articles.title: 🔢 The JSON Numbers JavaScript Quietly Corrupts
articles.description: JSON.parse changes your data and never says so. Three distinct failure modes, only one of which is the famous one about large integers.
articles.body_html:
Overview

This post will help identify the ways JSON.parse silently changes your data, and what you can do about it. We will cover why it happens, the three distinct failure modes it produces, how to check whether your own pipeline is affected, and the approach I use in my own tooling to prevent it. Each failure mode includes an example you can run in your browser console right now.

💡 Every example in this post takes less than ten seconds to verify. Open your console and follow along.

📚 Table of Contents

  • Why it happens
  • The three ways it bites
    • Large integers round
    • Overflow becomes null
    • Formatting is destroyed even when the value survives
  • What most tools do about it
  • What we do in Prettify
  • How to check whether this affects you
  • Drawbacks
  • The short version

First, try it yourself

Paste this into a browser console:

JSON.parse('{"id": 9007199254740993}').id

You get 9007199254740992. Off by one. No error, no warning, no truncation notice. The value you asked for is gone and something that looks just like it is standing where it was.

This is not a bug in JSON.parse. It is doing what the spec says. But it means that any JavaScript program that reads JSON, touches it, and writes it back is a program that can silently change your data, and most of them do not know it.

Why it happens

JSON has one numeric type and no size limit. The grammar is happy to describe a four-hundred-digit integer.

JavaScript also has one numeric type: the IEEE-754 double. It has 53 bits of integer precision. Past Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, which is 9007199254740991, consecutive integers stop being representable, and the parser rounds to whatever double is nearest.

So JSON.parse maps an unbounded numeric grammar onto a bounded numeric type. There is no way to do that without losing something, and the standard's choice is to lose it silently.

The three ways it bites

Value loss is the famous one. It is not the only one, and it is not the most common.

1. Large integers round 

JSON.parse('{"id": 1071004833782874112}').id
// 1071004833782874100

The last two digits are invented. That is a Discord-style snowflake ID, and the same applies to Twitter/X IDs, most database bigints, Stripe-style numeric identifiers, and anything else that packs a timestamp into a 64-bit integer.

🚧 The insidious part is that IDs are exactly the values where a near-miss is worse than a crash. A rounded price is obviously wrong. A rounded ID is a valid-looking ID that points at nothing, or worse, at something else.

2. Overflow becomes null 

JSON.parse('{"v": 1e400}').v
// Infinity

JSON.stringify(Infinity)
// "null"

Read a number too large for a double and you get Infinity. Write it back out and JSON.stringify turns Infinity into null, because JSON has no infinity literal.

So a round trip converts a number into a null. Downstream, that is not a precision problem. It is a type change, and whatever consumes the field next is going to be surprised.

3. Formatting is destroyed even when the value survives 

JSON.stringify(JSON.parse('{"v": 4.0}'))
// {"v":4}

4.0 and 4 are the same number. They are not the same document.

If you are round-tripping a config file, a fixture, an API contract, or anything a human wrote and will read again, 4.0 becoming 4 is a diff. It shows up in code review. It shows up in a git blame. Version-controlled JSON that a formatter "cleaned" is a classic source of noise commits.

The same goes for 1.00, -0 becoming 0, and 5e+3 becoming 5000.

And all three are silent

Nothing throws. Nothing logs. The document parses, the program runs, and the tests pass because the fixtures were generated by the same broken round trip.

You find out when a customer reports that a record will not load, and the ID in your logs is one digit off from the ID in theirs.

What most tools do about it

Nothing, mostly.

Every JSON formatter, viewer, and prettifier that works by calling JSON.parse and then JSON.stringify has all of these behaviors. That is the standard implementation. Paste a Discord message dump into a random online JSON formatter and the IDs come back wrong.

The workarounds people reach for:

  • Parse to BigInt. Handles large integers, does nothing for 4.0 or 1e400, and gives you a type that will not JSON.stringify without a custom replacer.
  • Parse numbers as strings. Safe, and it breaks every consumer that expected a number.
  • Ask the API for string IDs. Correct, and most public APIs already do this for exactly this reason. Also not available to you when you are just looking at somebody else's payload.

What we do in Prettify

The rule is: preserve the token, not the value.

When parsing, each numeric token gets one question asked about it. Would writing this back out produce the exact bytes I read? If yes, it stays an ordinary JavaScript number. If no, it becomes a wrapper that holds the original digit string.

The wrapper type and the two helpers below come from lossless-json. The policy around them is ours, and it is the part worth copying.

function parseNumber(value: string): number | LosslessNumber {
  if (isSafeNumber(value) && String(parseFloat(value)) === value) {
    return parseFloat(value)
  }
  return parseLosslessNumber(value)
}

Two conditions, because there are two independent failure modes, and this is the part that most implementations miss.

isSafeNumber catches value loss. It does not catch formatting loss: it says 4.0 is perfectly safe, because numerically it is. 4.0 and 4 are the same double.

That is why the second check exists. String(parseFloat("4.0")) is "4", which is not "4.0", so the token gets preserved even though nothing about its value was ever at risk.

💡 Checking only isSafeNumber is the natural implementation, and it silently reformats your document.

Wrap only what needs wrapping

The other half of the design is that most numbers are not wrapped. 1, 42, 0.1, -17.5 all stay ordinary numbers, because they round-trip exactly. Only the tokens that would change get the wrapper.

This matters for a reason that is more practical than philosophical: a wrapper is typeof === 'object'. Every typeof x === 'number' check in the codebase is false for it, and every "is this a container?" check is true for it unless you exclude it. Wrapping everything would mean auditing every numeric code path in the application. Wrapping only unsafe tokens keeps the blast radius to the small set of documents that actually contain them.

Viewing is not computing

Preserving a number exactly and doing arithmetic on it are incompatible goals in a language with one float type. So the two are separated by policy:

  • View, select, copy, round-trip: exact. The digits you pasted are the digits you get back.
  • Compute: coerced, and you are told. Arithmetic, aggregation, and comparison flatten to a float, because they have to. When that happens, the app says so.

That last clause is the whole point. The original sin of JSON.parse is not that it loses precision. It is that it loses precision without mentioning it. An answer you know is approximate is a usable answer. An answer you believe is exact and is not is a landmine.

How to check whether this affects you

Fastest test, in any JavaScript runtime:

const original = yourJsonString
const roundTripped = JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(original))
// If these differ, your pipeline is changing documents.

That catches all three cases at once, formatting included.

If it comes back different, the questions worth asking are: does anything downstream compare these documents, diff them, sign them, hash them, or use a numeric field as a key? If yes, you have a real problem rather than a cosmetic one.

Drawbacks

Being honest about the limits of this approach:

  • It only covers JSON and JSONL. The policy above applies to Prettify's JSON pipeline. YAML and CSV go through their own parsers and get ordinary JavaScript numbers, with all three behaviors described in this post.
  • Computing still coerces. Preserving a number exactly and doing math on it are incompatible in JavaScript. Arithmetic flattens to a float. The best a tool can do is tell you when it happened.
  • It does not help with data that was already corrupted upstream. If the ID was rounded before it reached you, no parser can recover the digits that were lost.

The short version

  • JSON.parse silently rounds integers past 9007199254740991
  • 1e400 round-trips to null, changing the type
  • 4.0 round-trips to 4, changing the document
  • None of it warns you
  • The fix is to preserve the original token when re-serializing it would differ, and to check formatting as well as value

Prettify preserves these numbers byte for byte, in JSON and JSONL, in the browser: paste a payload with a snowflake ID into the JSON viewer and the digits come back unchanged. The jq engine applies the same policy, and flags any query that had to coerce.

Happy Coding 🚀

Blog Post: https://prettify.tools/blog/the-json-numbers-javascript-corrupts

If you liked this content, follow me on Twitter @alexi_be3 💙

How to understand what AI wrote: For beginners!

Avoid lack of dopamine, mental atrophy, and other terrible things

You spin up a simple website quickly, and you want to understand what is actually happening, because you feel your sharpness drifting away in a sea of automation. What can be done? Here is one simple method I found that works for me: The simple comment.

Ask yourself some questions:

Can you go through the AI generated code line by line and understand what it is doing? Sure. But you have not really gone through it, have you? To really understand code, one must sit with it, digest it, and go on to the next part having the knowledge of what is happening so far. That investigative understanding is the part I feel many of us are missing. As a self proclaimed junior-ish developer, I miss the satisfaction of knowing I understand what just happened, and why it is working. I am certain developers of all experiences are feeling this now, based on the articles I have been reading.

🛏️ Anti-laziness movement

Now, I could have just committed the damn file, I knew it worked and was simple javascript. But this did not resonate well with me. Not this time. I went on a little side mission of commenting on every single line, explaining what each line was doing. I can tell you, I feel much better about it after doing so. Sure, it took 10 times as long. But who cares? I have a hamburger menu I can explain and share with others that are trying to learn. Do not auto-tab the comments or have AI write you comments that you are not going to read, that defeats the purpose. Type them out. Allow typos. Make mistakes. Above all... Learn!

Start with something simple

I dissected a simple hamburger menu, something that I am slightly obsessed with. Can we just appreciate the simple magnificence for one second?

=￣ω￣=

These have been around for ages and I am certain many of us use borrowed code or let AI do it. But what are we missing actually? I built a mockup website for a pretend business with simple HTML and CSS. Then I added javascript, admittedly my Achilles heel. An overwhelming amount of frameworks and cutting edge technologies leaves someone that is trying to learn in complete disarray. I had Claude write me up a hamburger menu that shows on small screens using vanilla javascript.

Pause before going forward

At this point I hit the breaks, and dissected the javascript. By slowing down and creating space for learning, a certain level of satisfaction and pride is returned to our work. Your coding experience does not always have to feel like: "Ahhhh! 500mph everything - new tech - no idea - must make work and do it fast!" This my friends, is the fast track to burnout, especially for those just beginning.

What it is actually doing:

For browsers that have javascript enabled, it creates the hamburger menu and a multi-select dropdown so users can select more than one event at a time. Small things like this, give us a real appreciation.

✨ Learning - Do not skip this part if you can find time

What I learned: does not support multi dropdown options, highlighting the use case of javascript here. What if I am a new user and want information on three events? Submitting 3 separate inquiries clogs up the whole user-support pipeline! Eww. However, it is good to know that in the edge case where users may have javascript disabled, they will still be able to select at least one option from the dropdown, allowing them to at least select something from the available options. That is a nice little built-in fall back feature! Here is the full javascript I used for the hamburger menu and navbar UI components. Of course you will need some CSS and HTML So I’ve stripped down the website to bare bones for demonstration purposes only. Been a minute since I used codepen! There are alot of comments, I reccommend going to codepen and making your screen super wide. 🤣

Everyone is of course welcome to use my example. No need to ask. 👾 The point of all of this is that the root of our satisfaction comes from knowing why things are working and understanding on a deep level. I have never had a project manager, but I would have to say I'd be better equipped to explain things to others in ways they can understand if I understand technically speaking, the whys and the wherefores of what is possible, or not.

articles.title: Claude Code File System Boundaries in 2026: What `--add-dir`, Allowed Paths, and Sandbox Roots Actually Restrict
articles.description: Claude Code's filesystem permissions operate on two distinct layers that most teams conflate. Understanding the difference between sandbox roots and allowed paths determines whether your agent can read secrets, overwrite production config, or execute
articles.body_html:
Claude Code File System Boundaries in 2026: What --add-dir, Allowed Paths, and Sandbox Roots Actually Restrict

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

The Filesystem Permission Model Nobody Reads

Teams enable Claude Code in production repositories with --add-dir flags they copied from documentation, then discover the agent reading .env files or modifying sibling project directories during auto mode. The failure stems from conflating two independent permission layers that operate at different abstraction levels.

Problem flow showing Claude Code reading secrets due to misconfigured permissions

The correct model separates sandbox roots (which directories the Bash tool can execute commands inside) from allowed paths (which files Claude's read/write tools can access directly). Configuring one layer does not constrain the other.

Solution flow showing properly isolated permissions

This post dissects the boundary mechanics teams must internalize before granting auto-approve permissions. The difference between a contained agent and one that leaks credentials sits in understanding these two layers.

Key Takeaways

  • Sandbox roots (controlled by --add-dir and additionalDirectories) determine where Bash commands execute, while allowed paths (controlled by allowRead, allowEdit, denyRead, denyEdit) govern which files Claude's tools can access directly.
  • Adding allowRead: ['.'] to re-enable project access also re-exposes every file under the working directory, including .env and secrets/, unless explicitly denied in the same configuration block.
  • Bash commands inherit sandbox root permissions, not allowed path rules, meaning a cat .env command succeeds even when .env sits in a denied path.
  • The --add-dir flag expands the sandbox perimeter but does not automatically grant file read/write permissions to those directories for Claude's direct tools.
  • Production configurations must deny secret paths explicitly and constrain sandbox roots to the minimum set of directories where build/test commands legitimately need write access.

Understanding --add-dir and additionalDirectories: What Actually Gets Unlocked

The --add-dir flag controls sandbox root expansion. When a developer starts Claude Code with claude-code --add-dir ../shared-utils, the Bash sandbox gains write access to that directory. Commands like cd ../shared-utils && npm install now succeed because the sandbox boundary extends to include that path.

This permission operates at the process execution layer. The Bash tool can create, modify, and delete files anywhere inside a sandbox root. No allowRead or allowEdit configuration constrains what happens inside a bash_tool invocation.

Diagram showing sandbox root expansion with --add-dir flag

The additionalDirectories field in a permission configuration file (.claude/permissions.jsonc) provides the same capability programmatically. Both mechanisms add paths to the sandbox root set, which starts with the working directory and a per-user temp directory by default.

The trap appears when teams assume that adding a directory to the sandbox automatically grants Claude's read_file or write_file tools permission to access those files. It does not. A --add-dir ../secrets flag allows Bash commands to manipulate that directory, but Claude cannot directly read or write files there unless the allowed paths configuration explicitly permits it.

Conversely, granting allowRead: ['../secrets'] without adding that directory as a sandbox root means Claude can read files directly, but any Bash command that attempts to cd ../secrets fails because the sandbox boundary blocks it. The layers operate independently.

Sandbox Roots vs Allowed Paths: The Layer Distinction That Bites

Sandbox roots define where processes can execute. Allowed paths define which files Claude's tools can touch. The confusion costs teams hours when an agent behavior seems inconsistent, reading some files but not others, or executing commands in unexpected directories.

Two-layer permission model showing sandbox roots and allowed paths

A concrete scenario clarifies the split. A repository contains three directories: src/, tests/, and secrets/. The developer starts Claude Code with --add-dir ./tests and configures:

{
  "allowRead": ["./src"],
  "allowEdit": ["./src"],
  "denyRead": ["./secrets"]
}

Claude can directly read and write files under src/ using its read/write tools. When asked to run the test suite, the agent executes bash_tool with cd tests && npm test, which succeeds because tests/ sits inside a sandbox root. If the agent tries to read tests/utils.test.ts using read_file, the operation fails because tests/ does not appear in allowRead.

The secrets/ directory sits outside both layers. Claude cannot read it directly (denied), and no Bash command can access it (not a sandbox root). This configuration achieves the intended isolation.

Claude Code permission layers diagram showing sandbox and allowed path boundaries

The failure mode emerges when teams add allowRead: ['.'] to fix a perceived overly restrictive setup. That single line re-exposes every file under the working directory to Claude's read tool, including secrets/, unless an explicit denyRead rule blocks it. The sandbox root layer remains unchanged, but the allowed paths layer just opened wide.

Code Example: Testing Filesystem Boundaries in Practice

A test script proves the layer separation. The setup creates a directory structure with files at different permission levels, then attempts operations through both Bash and direct file tools.

// verify-boundaries.ts
import { execSync } from 'child_process';
import { writeFileSync, readFileSync, mkdirSync } from 'fs';
import { join } from 'path';

// Setup test structure
const testRoot = './boundary-test';
mkdirSync(join(testRoot, 'allowed'), { recursive: true });
mkdirSync(join(testRoot, 'sandbox-only'), { recursive: true });
mkdirSync(join(testRoot, 'blocked'), { recursive: true });

writeFileSync(join(testRoot, 'allowed', 'public.txt'), 'safe content');
writeFileSync(join(testRoot, 'sandbox-only', 'build.log'), 'build output');
writeFileSync(join(testRoot, 'blocked', 'secret.key'), 'credential');

// Test 1: Direct read tool on allowed path
try {
  const content = readFileSync(join(testRoot, 'allowed', 'public.txt'), 'utf-8');
  console.log('✓ read_file on allowed path:', content);
} catch (err) {
  console.log('✗ read_file blocked:', err.message);
}

// Test 2: Direct read tool on sandbox-only path (not in allowRead)
try {
  const content = readFileSync(join(testRoot, 'sandbox-only', 'build.log'), 'utf-8');
  console.log('✓ read_file on sandbox-only:', content);
} catch (err) {
  console.log('✗ read_file blocked on sandbox-only:', err.message);
}

// Test 3: Bash command on sandbox-only path
try {
  const output = execSync(`cat ${join(testRoot, 'sandbox-only', 'build.log')}`, {
    encoding: 'utf-8',
    cwd: testRoot
  });
  console.log('✓ bash_tool on sandbox-only:', output);
} catch (err) {
  console.log('✗ bash_tool blocked:', err.message);
}

// Test 4: Bash command on blocked path (outside sandbox)
try {
  const output = execSync(`cat ${join(testRoot, 'blocked', 'secret.key')}`, {
    encoding: 'utf-8',
    cwd: testRoot
  });
  console.log('✓ bash_tool on blocked path:', output);
} catch (err) {
  console.log('✗ bash_tool blocked on denied path');
}

Running this script with the configuration from the previous section demonstrates the boundary enforcement. Test 1 succeeds because the file sits in an allowed path. Test 2 fails because sandbox-only/ does not appear in allowRead, even though it sits inside a sandbox root. Test 3 succeeds because Bash can execute inside sandbox roots regardless of allowed paths. Test 4 fails because blocked/ sits outside the sandbox boundary entirely.

The output proves that adding a directory to sandbox roots does not grant file tool access, and vice versa. Teams that skip this verification step deploy agents with permissions they did not intend to grant.

Why allowRead: ['.'] Re-Exposes Secrets and How to Deny Them Correctly

The pattern allowRead: ['.'] appears in permission files when developers encounter repeated "permission denied" errors during development. The wildcard grants read access to every file under the working directory, which includes configuration files, environment variables, and any secrets stored in the repository.

A repository with this structure demonstrates the risk:

project/
├── src/
├── tests/
├── .env
├── secrets/
│   └── api-keys.json
└── .claude/
    └── permissions.jsonc

The following configuration seems safe because it denies the secrets/ directory:

{
  "allowRead": ["."],
  "denyRead": ["secrets/"]
}

Claude cannot read secrets/api-keys.json because the deny rule takes precedence. But .env sits directly in the working directory, fully exposed. The agent can read database credentials, API tokens, and any other environment secrets without restriction.

Permission flow showing how allowRead re-exposes secrets

The fix requires enumerating every secret path and denying it explicitly:

{
  "allowRead": ["."],
  "denyRead": [
    ".env",
    ".env.*",
    "secrets/",
    "*.key",
    "*.pem",
    "*.p12"
  ]
}

This approach scales poorly. Every new secret file type requires a configuration update. A safer pattern allows only the directories that Claude legitimately needs to read:

{
  "allowRead": [
    "src/",
    "tests/",
    "package.json",
    "tsconfig.json"
  ],
  "allowEdit": ["src/"],
  "denyRead": ["*"],  // explicit default-deny
  "denyEdit": ["*"]
}

The explicit default-deny rule makes the permission model fail-safe. Adding a new directory to the repository does not automatically grant access. Teams must consciously expand the allowed set, forcing a review of what the agent can reach.

Bash Commands vs Claude Tools: Which Permissions Block What

The permission model enforces different rules depending on whether Claude invokes a Bash command or calls a direct file tool. Understanding which layer blocks which operation prevents the "it worked in the shell but failed in the agent" confusion.

Comparison of Bash tool and file tool permission enforcement

Operation Layer Checked Fails When Succeeds When
bash_tool: cat file.txt Sandbox roots File outside sandbox boundary File in any sandbox root
read_file: file.txt Allowed paths File not in allowRead or in denyRead File in allowRead and not denied
bash_tool: cd ../other && ls Sandbox roots ../other outside sandbox ../other added via --add-dir
write_file: file.txt Allowed paths File not in allowEdit or in denyEdit File in allowEdit and not denied

A practical scenario illustrates the split. A monorepo contains apps/web and packages/shared. The developer starts Claude Code from apps/web with:

claude-code --add-dir ../../packages/shared

The configuration file specifies:

{
  "allowRead": ["./src"],
  "allowEdit": ["./src"]
}

When Claude needs to build the app, it executes:

bash_tool: cd ../../packages/shared && npm run build

This command succeeds because packages/shared sits in a sandbox root. The build writes output to packages/shared/dist, which also succeeds because Bash operates inside the sandbox boundary.

If Claude then tries to read the build output directly:

read_file: ../../packages/shared/dist/index.js

The operation fails. The file sits outside the allowed read paths. The sandbox layer permitted the build, but the allowed paths layer blocks the read. The agent must use bash_tool: cat ../../packages/shared/dist/index.js to access the content, which routes through the sandbox layer instead.

Diagram showing different permission enforcement for Bash versus direct file tools

Teams encounter this pattern when CI scripts rely on build artifacts that the agent cannot read directly. The solution either adds the artifact directory to allowRead or restructures the workflow to keep everything inside allowed paths, eliminating the sandbox-only zone.

Production Patterns: Locking Down Your Agent Before Auto Mode

Production deployments require a defense-in-depth model that assumes the agent will attempt operations outside its intended scope. The configuration must fail safely when Claude requests access to an unexpected path.

Production permission lockdown flow

The baseline configuration for a Next.js application running automated testing looks like:

{
  "additionalDirectories": [],  // only working directory
  "allowRead": [
    "app/",
    "components/",
    "lib/",
    "public/",
    "package.json",
    "next.config.js",
    "tsconfig.json",
    "playwright.config.ts"
  ],
  "allowEdit": [
    "app/",
    "components/",
    "lib/"
  ],
  "denyRead": [
    ".env*",
    "secrets/",
    "*.key",
    "*.pem",
    "node_modules/",
    ".next/",
    "coverage/"
  ],
  "denyEdit": [
    "package.json",
    "*.config.*",
    ".github/",
    "README.md"
  ]
}

This setup grants the agent read access to source directories and configuration files it needs to understand the codebase. Write permissions limit to source code only. Build artifacts, dependencies, and configuration files sit in deny lists.

The additionalDirectories field remains empty, constraining Bash commands to the working directory. If the agent needs to run tests that write temporary files, those writes succeed because the working directory sits in the default sandbox root set. External directories remain unreachable.

The explicit deny rules prevent accidental exposure if a developer later adds allowRead: ['.'] during debugging. The deny list takes precedence, maintaining the security boundary even when the allow list expands.

A stricter variant for CI environments removes all write permissions:

{
  "additionalDirectories": [],
  "allowRead": [
    "app/",
    "components/",
    "lib/",
    "package.json",
    "playwright.config.ts"
  ],
  "allowEdit": [],  // no direct file writes
  "denyRead": ["*"],
  "denyEdit": ["*"]
}

The agent can read source code and configuration but cannot modify files directly. Test runs that need to write output must use bash_tool commands, which remain constrained to the working directory sandbox. This configuration supports agents that analyze codebases and run tests but cannot make changes autonomously.

Teams deploying auto-approve modes must start from this restrictive baseline and expand permissions only when a specific, verified use case demands it. The expansion process requires documenting why each path needs access and what risk it introduces.

For more details on broader permission strategies, see Claude Code Permission Modes, allowedTools, and Sandbox Configuration.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does adding a directory with --add-dir grant Claude read access to files inside it?

No. The --add-dir flag expands the sandbox root set, which controls where Bash commands can execute. Claude's read_file and write_file tools remain governed by the allowed paths configuration. A file can sit inside a sandbox root but still be inaccessible to direct file tools if it does not appear in allowRead.

Can Claude read .env if it sits outside the sandbox roots but inside allowed paths?

Yes. The allowed paths layer operates independently from sandbox roots. If allowRead: ['.env'] appears in the configuration, Claude can read that file directly even if it sits outside every sandbox root. Bash commands attempting to cat .env would fail if .env sits outside the sandbox, but the read_file tool succeeds because it checks a different layer.

What happens when both allowRead and denyRead match the same file?

Deny rules take precedence. If a file matches both allowRead: ['.'] and denyRead: ['.env'], the deny rule blocks access. This precedence enables safe use of broad allow patterns with specific exceptions for sensitive files.

Why does npm install work but read_file: node_modules/package/index.js fail?

The npm install command runs through bash_tool, which operates inside sandbox roots. The working directory sits in the default sandbox root set, so the command succeeds. Reading a file under node_modules/ requires an explicit allowRead entry for that path. The sandbox layer permitted the install, but the allowed paths layer blocks the read.

Should production configurations use allowRead: ['.'] with extensive deny lists?

No. Production configurations should enumerate allowed paths explicitly and use denyRead: ['*'] as a default-deny rule. The allow-with-exceptions pattern scales poorly and introduces risk when new files appear in the repository. Explicit allow lists force conscious permission expansion and make the security model auditable.

The Two-Layer Model You Must Internalize

Sandbox roots control where processes execute. Allowed paths control which files tools can touch directly. Conflating these layers leads to agents that leak secrets or fail mysteriously when permissions seem correctly configured. Production deployments require explicit allow lists, default-deny rules, and documentation of why each path needs access. The boundary between contained and compromised sits in understanding that --add-dir and allowRead operate on different mechanisms entirely. Teams that treat filesystem permissions as a single unified model will spend hours debugging behavior that the two-layer architecture explains immediately.

For guidance on structuring agent workflows within these boundaries, see Claude Code CI: Agentic Review, Test, and Auto-Fix Workflows and Claude Code Cost Control in Production: Rate Limits, Budgets, and Safe Auto-Approve.

I was building Crowdwide, a social media platform I started for new indie devs, smaller communities, and smaller creators to raise their voices higher.

Your voice shouldn't be judged based on how big a platform you join. Everyone's voice should be equal.

And today is Day 21 of building Crowdwide!!!

YESSSSS!! 🔥🔥

Crowdwide is in a mostly stable state now! Its core features, main algorithm, mailing system, and recommendation system, Widewave, are finally DONE!

So now, it's time to polish the UI.

On Day 21, I'm just polishing the UI of Crowdwide.

The things I thought needed the most improvement were the background color combination, theme adaptability, and sidebar (THIS NEEDS HEAVY IMPROVEMENT!).

The background used to have gradients, but when users scrolled a lot, the background stretched and created a weird shade at the top.

articles.title: My Instagram tool's traffic was 82% Indonesian — so I taught it WhatsApp
articles.description: Search Console told me my Instagram chat analyzer's audience was mostly Indonesian — and WhatsApp-first — while the tool only spoke Instagram. This is the messy parsing work of fixing that.
articles.body_html:
The Search Console export that rewrote my roadmap

Stats Insta is a small tool I built for myself and then put online: upload an Instagram chat export, get statistics about your conversations — who texts most, when you're active, your top emojis, Wrapped-style story cards you can share. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded anywhere.

A few weeks ago I finally did the boring thing and exported sixteen months of Google Search Console data to actually look at it. Around 6,500 clicks. And 82% of them from Indonesia.

It gets stranger. Most of my top search queries weren't keywords at all — they were people typing my old Vercel domain name into Google to find their way back. Traffic had peaked back in December 2025 (Wrapped season, of course) and was slowly sliding. In other words: the tool had found an audience almost by accident, the audience was Indonesian, and it was loyal enough to Google a URL.

Here's the part that stung: Indonesia is a WhatsApp-first country. For most of my actual users, WhatsApp is not "an app" — it's the default layer for talking to everyone. And my tool supported exactly zero WhatsApp. Every one of those users was analyzing the chats they have on their secondary app, because the app they actually live in wasn't supported at all.

So the roadmap rewrote itself. Before any new features: teach the tool WhatsApp.

Two parsers, two completely different worlds

Instagram exports are a gift. You request your data, wait, and get message_1.json — real structured JSON with sender_name, timestamp_ms, a reactions array, the works. Parsing it is an afternoon.

A WhatsApp export is a .txt file that looks like a chat transcript, because it is one:

14/08/2025, 21:03 - Messages are end-to-end encrypted
14/08/2025, 21:04 - Priya: ok so about tomorrow
[14/08/2025, 21:04:37] Arjun: wait, which tomorrow?

That first line is Android format, the third is iOS. Neither is a standard — the comma is optional, seconds come and go, and the clock is 12-hour in some regions and 24-hour in others. The parser ended up starting with two regexes just to recognize a line:

const IOS_LINE =
  /^\[(\d{1,2})[./](\d{1,2})[./](\d{2,4}),?\s+(\d{1,2}):(\d{2})(?::(\d{2}))?\s*([AaPp]\.?[Mm]\.?)?\]\s?(.*)$/;
const ANDROID_LINE =
  /^(\d{1,2})[./](\d{1,2})[./](\d{2,4}),?\s+(\d{1,2}):(\d{2})(?::(\d{2}))?\s*([AaPp]\.?[Mm]\.?)?\s*[-\u2010-\u2015]\s+(.*)$/;

Then the real problems start:

Half the lines aren't messages. The encryption notice, "Priya added Arjun", subject changes, "security code changed", missed calls — all of it sits in the file wearing a timestamp, and all of it has to be excluded or your statistics count WhatsApp itself as a very talkative participant.

Some system lines disguise themselves as messages. Alice changed the subject to "Trip: Friday plans" contains a ": " — so a naive split happily parses it as a message from a person named "Alice changed the subject to "Trip". I ended up treating a "sender" as fake if it's implausibly long or contains a system verb before the colon.

Multi-line messages have no prefix at all. If someone sends a message with line breaks, the continuation lines arrive naked. The rule is simple — a line with no timestamp belongs to the previous message — but you only discover that after your message count doesn't match the chat you exported by hand.

The file is full of invisible characters. A BOM at the start, narrow no-break spaces before AM/PM, left-to-right marks wrapped around lines. Normalize them away first, or your regexes fail on files that look identical to the ones that work.

And the worst one: nobody tells you the date order. Is 03/04/2025 the 3rd of April or March 4th? WhatsApp doesn't label it, and guessing wrong swaps days and months across the entire history. The parser scans the whole file before parsing anything:

let dayFirst = true;
let sawMonthFirstEvidence = false;
for (const line of lines) {
  const raw = matchTimestampLine(line);
  if (!raw) continue;
  if (raw.first > 12) { dayFirst = true; break; } // 13+ can't be a month
  if (raw.second > 12) sawMonthFirstEvidence = true;
}
if (sawMonthFirstEvidence) dayFirst = false;

If any date's first number is above 12, it must be the day. If only the second number ever goes above 12, the file is month-first. If the file never gives unambiguous evidence — a short chat from the first twelve days of a month — it defaults to day-first, which matches the export locales of most of my users: Indonesia, India, Europe, Latin America. It's a heuristic, and I wrote it down as one in the code comments, because pretending it's a guarantee would be lying.

One stats engine, two front doors

The best decision in the whole project was refusing to build a second analyzer. The WhatsApp parser's only job is to normalize a messy text file into the exact same shape the Instagram path already produces:

{ [sender_name: string]: Message[] }

Because the model is identical, every existing statistic, chart and story card — totals, distribution, the activity heatmap, night owls, conversation starters — worked on WhatsApp chats the moment the parser did. Zero changes downstream.

The only additions were three optional flags on Message, and they turned out to be where the fun was:

  • isDeleted — "This message was deleted" arrives under the sender's name, so instead of discarding it, the parser keeps it as a flagged, content-less message. It counts toward that person's totals but is invisible to text statistics. That's what powers a Deleted Messages leaderboard — who in your group chat deletes the most.
  • isMedia — <Media omitted>, <attached: IMG-2041.jpg>, IMG-2041.jpg (file attached) (captions kept, when there are any). Powers Media Shared counts.
  • isEdited — WhatsApp appends <This message was edited> to edited messages, sometimes on its own line. The parser strips the marker and flags the message.

From those flags plus the plain text fell out a set of stats that make no sense for Instagram but are pure WhatsApp: Top Link Sharers, Questions Asked (who asks the most questions), Biggest Double-Texter, plus Signature Emoji, Fastest Responder (average reply gaps) and Morning Person. One graceful accident: WhatsApp exports carry no reaction data, so reaction-based stats simply find nothing — exactly what they already did for an Instagram chat where nobody reacted. Nothing needed special-casing.

What shipped

The tool now takes Instagram JSON and WhatsApp .txt/ZIP exports through the same upload box, tells them apart on its own, and runs the same engine on both. There's a dedicated WhatsApp page, WhatsApp-specific cards, a downloadable report, and Wrapped story cards that now say "WhatsApp" when they're about a WhatsApp chat (a detail I got wrong in the first version, and a user caught within hours — platform support means the copy, not just the parser).

Is it too early for a victory lap? Completely. The honest result so far is: the tool finally supports the app its audience actually uses. Whether the December slide reverses is a question the next Search Console export will answer, and I've learned my lesson about reading those more often.

If you want to try it — everything runs locally in your browser, your chats never leave your device:

  • The tool: https://stats-insta.vercel.app
  • WhatsApp chat analyzer: https://stats-insta.vercel.app/whatsapp-chat-analyzer
  • Guide — how to export a WhatsApp chat: https://stats-insta.vercel.app/guides/export-whatsapp-chat

And if you've ever parsed WhatsApp exports yourself and fought the date-order problem differently, I genuinely want to hear how. The comments are open.

articles.title: What "non-manifold" actually means in an STL file (and how to count the problems yourself)
articles.description: Every slicer has a moment where it pops up "this model has errors" and offers to fix them. Most of...
articles.body_html:
Every slicer has a moment where it pops up "this model has errors" and offers to fix them. Most of the time you click yes, the print comes out fine, and you never think about it again. But when the auto-fix guesses wrong (a vent sealed shut, two parts fused, a wall that just isn't there), it helps to know what the slicer was actually complaining about.

The good news: the checks behind those warnings are simple. You can reason about them with nothing more than a list of triangles.

An STL is just triangles

An STL file has no curves, no units, and no idea which triangles belong together. It's a flat list of triangles, each with three corner points and a normal. Even the corners aren't shared: if six triangles meet at one point, that point is written six times.

That last detail matters, because every check below is about how triangles connect, and the file doesn't store connections at all. You have to rebuild them.

Step 1: weld the duplicate corners

Before you can ask "which triangles share this edge?", you need to know which corners are the same point. The usual approach is to round each coordinate to a tolerance and treat matching positions as one vertex:

// positions: Float32Array, 9 numbers per triangle (3 corners × xyz)
const TOL = 1e-6;
const ids = new Map();
const key = (x, y, z) =>
  `${Math.round(x / TOL)},${Math.round(y / TOL)},${Math.round(z / TOL)}`;

const index = [];
for (let i = 0; i < positions.length; i += 3) {
  const k = key(positions[i], positions[i + 1], positions[i + 2]);
  if (!ids.has(k)) ids.set(k, ids.size);
  index.push(ids.get(k));
}
// index now has 3 vertex ids per triangle

Welding doesn't change the shape. It only recovers the topology the format threw away.

Step 2: count how many triangles use each edge

With shared vertex ids, every triangle has three edges, and an edge is just a pair of ids. Sort the pair so A–B and B–A are the same edge, then count:

const edgeUse = new Map();
for (let t = 0; t < index.length; t += 3) {
  const [a, b, c] = [index[t], index[t + 1], index[t + 2]];
  for (const [u, v] of [[a, b], [b, c], [c, a]]) {
    const e = u < v ? `${u}_${v}` : `${v}_${u}`;
    edgeUse.set(e, (edgeUse.get(e) || 0) + 1);
  }
}

Now the three classic problems fall out of that one map.

The three things your slicer is warning about

1. Holes (boundary edges). An edge used by exactly one triangle is on the rim of an opening. A closed shell has none. A model straight out of a sculpting app with an unfinished base, or a scan that missed the underside, will have a whole loop of them.

2. Non-manifold edges. An edge used by three or more triangles. Picture two boxes that touch along one edge, or an internal wall left over from a boolean. The slicer can no longer tell which side is inside, which is where missing walls and odd infill come from.

3. Degenerate triangles. Triangles with (near) zero area: two corners in the same spot, or all three in a line. They're usually harmless leftovers from exports, but they can trip up the edge analysis and some slicers' repair passes.

"Watertight", in the sense slicers mean it, is simply: every edge is used by exactly two triangles.

What a basic repair can safely do, and what it shouldn't

Some fixes are safe because they don't invent geometry:

  • Weld near-duplicate vertices (same shape, cleaner data)
  • Drop zero-area triangles
  • Recompute normals so the preview shades correctly

Filling holes is different. A fill has to make up surface that isn't in the file, and an automatic fill has no idea whether that opening was a mistake or a vent you meant to keep. That's a decision for a tool where you can see and undo the result: your slicer's repair, Blender's fill on a boundary loop, or Meshmixer.

There are also problems an edge count simply can't see: triangles that pass through each other without sharing an edge (self-intersections), and a shell whose triangles are wound inside-out. If a model passes the edge test and still slices strangely, those are the next suspects.

Trying it on your own file

If you'd rather not write the script, I put this exact check in a browser page: STL repair check. It counts holes, non-manifold edges, degenerate triangles and duplicate vertices, runs the safe basic repair above, and gives you a repaired STL. The file is parsed in the tab and never uploaded. It deliberately does not fill holes, for the reason above.

One related trap: if your file is huge because of triangle count rather than detail, slicing is slow and repair tools choke. Reducing the triangle count first, then running the check, is often the faster path. Decimation can open small gaps, so check after reducing, not before.

Quick reference

Edge used by… Meaning Usual cause
1 triangle Hole / open boundary Unfinished base, scan gap, deleted face
2 triangles Normal, watertight —
3+ triangles Non-manifold Touching parts, leftover internal walls

If you've ever had a slicer "fix" eat part of a model, I'd like to hear what the original problem turned out to be. Did the repair check agree with your slicer?

articles.title: Your image sitemap is already a social media feed
articles.description: I was about to build a publishing queue. The image sitemap I generate for Googlebot already was one — image, caption and canonical URL per book, always current.
articles.body_html:
Every image sitemap I have ever written was a thing I produced for crawlers and then never read again. It turns out mine had been quietly maintaining a publishing queue for months, and I only noticed when I went to build one.

The thing I was about to build

I wanted a small job that posts one illustrated page a day to Bluesky and Mastodon: the artwork, a line of the story, and a link back to the book.

The plan was the obvious one — query the database for books, join the illustrations, pull a caption from somewhere, render a queue. A day of work, a new table, another thing to keep in sync with the site.

The thing that already existed

Then I actually opened the sitemap we publish for Google Images:

<url>
  <loc>https://thewonderbooks.com/app/comics/book/astral_echoes_scars_of_tomorrow</loc>
  <image:image>
    <image:loc>.../covers/astral_echoes_cover_large.webp</image:loc>
    <image:title>Astral Echoes: Scars of Tomorrow — book cover</image:title>
  </image:image>
  <image:image>
    <image:loc>.../illustrations/astral_echoes_page_01.webp</image:loc>
    <image:caption>The Painted Desert shimmered under twin suns, its sands
      swirling with colors unknown on Earth.</image:caption>
  </image:image>
  ...
</url>

Per book, in one file, already public, already correct:

  • the canonical reader URL
  • the cover
  • every page illustration
  • and image:caption — which, because of how the sitemap is generated, is the sentence printed on that page of the book

That is a post. Image, copy, destination. The caption is better than anything I would have written for a social post, because it is the actual prose a reader sees.

So the "pipeline" became a fetch and a parse:

const xml = await fetch(`${SITE}/sitemaps/library-en.xml`).then(r => r.text());
const books = xml.split('<url>').slice(1).map(parseUrlBlock).filter(Boolean);

2,036 book pages with artwork in English, and the same again in twelve more languages. No new table, no second source of truth, and it cannot drift from the site — if a book is not published, it is not in the sitemap, so it cannot be posted.

Three things that bit me anyway

1. The sitemap is XML, so the URLs are escaped. A storage URL arrived as ?alt=media&token=… and answered 403. I was unescaping captions and not hrefs. I found it by HEAD-ing every queued URL before posting — 24 checks, one bad — rather than by trusting the exit code.

2. A "cover" is not always where you think. Most covers lived under /covers/, so I keyed on the path. Some books use their page-1 illustration as the cover, marked only by its caption reading — book cover —. Those posted as if they were inside pages, using "Title — book cover — Library" as the story line. Read the caption first, the path second.

3. Link cards and image embeds are not the same post. On Bluesky I attached the artwork as an external card thumbnail and left the URL in the text. The card already shows the title, the description and the domain, so the raw URL wrapped mid-slug across two lines underneath a card that said the same thing. The card is clickable on its own. Delete the URL from the text.

All three were found by looking at the published post, not by reading logs. The logs were green for every one of them.

The general version

If you publish a sitemap with image: extensions, you already have a structured, deduplicated, always-current feed of every piece of media you own, with human-written captions attached, keyed to canonical URLs. You built it for Googlebot. It works just as well for anything else that needs "an image, a line, and a link".

Worth opening yours before you build the thing you think you need.

I build WonderBooks — twelve free illustrated libraries in thirteen languages. The sitemap above is the real one.

articles.title: Canopy: Rewarding Laziness in Git Workflows with On-Demand Slices and Semantic Caching
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady Drafted...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady
Drafted on DEV via DevRelay MCP: Edit on DEV

What I Built

Cloning a multi-gigabyte monorepo just to inspect one file or understand a recent change wastes gigabytes of bandwidth and minutes of developer time. I built Canopy (live at https://canopy-lazy-git.onrender.com) to reward developer laziness: instead of downloading thousands of untouched blobs upfront, it mounts repositories using 767-byte manifest slices and materializes files strictly on demand. When you ask for diff digests, commit messages, or component architecture, Canopy derives the answer once with Google Gemma, validates it through Zod, and caches it permanently in SQLite for instant warm reads.

The Problem: Monorepos Punish Curiosity

In large monorepos, traditional developer tools demand total commitment up front. You want to check what changed in the billing service? Run git clone, wait several minutes, pull down hundreds of megabytes of history, and watch your laptop fan spin.

Anthropic's Scion explored making git lazy for autonomous AI agents. Canopy makes a repository lazy for human developers, backed by an open-weight model and content-addressed local caching that you control.

Key Capabilities

  • Lazy Slice-Based Filesystem (src/cli/client.ts): canopy mount fetches only the root directory manifest slice (767 bytes). Sub-directories and file blobs are resolved on demand and cached in .canopy/objects/ using their SHA-1 hashes. Subsequent reads hit local disk in 25.7 ms with 0 network bytes.
  • Bilingual Repository Digest (canopy digest): Generates an authoritative two-line summary and potential risk flags for recent commit ranges (e.g. HEAD~5) in either English or Bengali (--lang bn).
  • Architectural Role Explanation (canopy why <path>): Analyzes git commit history, file blame, and author distributions to explain a component's primary role and evolution patterns.
  • Commit Message Synthesizer (canopy commit): Derives concise, conventional commit titles and bodies from staged diffs piped via stdin.
  • Boot-Time Demo Cache Warmer (src/server/warmer.ts): Pre-warms key digests and architecture files on boot, dropping initial user latency from ~13.7s to ~4ms (a 3,400x speedup).
  • Sentry GenAI Agent Tracing (src/server/sentry.ts): Instruments every LLM call across four designated agents (CanopyDigestAgent, CanopyWhyAgent, CanopyCommitAgent, CanopySummaryAgent) following OpenTelemetry semantic conventions, with strict developer privacy that scrubs client IP addresses and diff payloads.

Demo

Experience Canopy directly in your browser:

  • 🌐 Live Web Application: https://canopy-lazy-git.onrender.com
  • ⚡ Zero-Wait Demo Experience: Explore the interactive tree viewer, inspect code blobs with cached AI summaries, toggle between English and Bengali digests, inspect architectural why files, and view real-time GenAI trace telemetry.

  • Walkthrough Video: docs/demo.webm (WebM, 1280x720, 86s, 5.40 MB)
  • High-Resolution GIF: docs/demo.gif (540x304, 0.91 MB)

Code

SayemR0018 / canopy

A lazy, AI-assisted layer over git

Canopy 🌲

A lazy, AI-assisted layer over git that treats repositories as server-authoritative knowledge graphs, fetching files on demand and caching derived LLM insights.

Built for the dev.to Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: "Slow and Steady" (rewarding laziness in developer workflows).

The Concept: Lazy Repositories for Lazy Developers & Agents

Modern monorepos and sprawling codebases waste gigabytes of bandwidth and minutes of developer time during full clones, even when an engineer or AI agent only needs to read 5 files and understand recent changes.

Canopy is inspired by the architecture described in Anthropic's public post, "Redesigning source control at Anthropic" (Scion), along with ideas from Meta's Sapling and Mononoke:

  • Server-Authoritative Tree: Clients do not clone full git commit graphs or download historical packfiles upfront.
  • Lazy Hydration: The client mounts a lightweight tree manifest. Blobs are fetched only when read (canopy cat or UI file view) and…
View on GitHub
  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/SayemR0018/canopy
  • License: Permissive MIT License
  • Tech Stack: Node >= 22.5.0, TypeScript, Hono, Dual SQLite Adapter (node:sqlite / better-sqlite3 with WAL mode), Google Gemma 4 (models/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it), Sentry, Docker, Render.

The Lazy Payoff: Real Benchmark Numbers

To measure real-world performance without network variance, Canopy includes a deterministic synthetic repository generator (scripts/seed.ts) producing 3,000 files across 40 directories and 200 commits in under 2 seconds.

Every number below comes directly from our 7-iteration benchmark script (scripts/benchmark.ts), audited automatically by scripts/check-claims.ts:

Metric Traditional Git Clone (history) Working Tree Baseline Canopy Lazy Layer (Median) Difference / Savings
Initial Operation Time 1,858 ms (git clone) N/A 266 ms (canopy mount) 7x faster initial setup (min: 250 ms, max: 334 ms)
Initial Download Size 2,908,949 bytes (2.77 MiB) 1,486,369 bytes (1.42 MiB) 767 bytes (0.7 KiB) 100% initial bandwidth saved (root slice)
Cold Read (5 files) Included in clone Included in working tree 1,102 ms (1,937 bytes / 1.9 KiB) Selective on-demand fetch (min: 1,080 ms, max: 1,243 ms)
Warm Read (5 files) Filesystem cache Filesystem cache 25.7 ms (0 network bytes) Local content-addressed cache (min: 22.8 ms, max: 28.8 ms)
Total Transfer (5 files) 2,908,949 bytes (2.77 MiB) 1,486,369 bytes (1.42 MiB) 2,704 bytes (2.6 KiB) 99.9% savings vs clone (99.8% vs tree)
Total Time (Mount + 5 files) 1,858 ms N/A 1,368 ms 1.4x faster end-to-end

Baselines Explained

We benchmark Canopy against two standard baselines: Full Git Clone (with history), which measures the complete network and disk footprint of cloning the repository including all historical packfiles, commit objects, and the working tree (2.77 MiB); and Working Tree Size, which measures only the raw uncompressed bytes of the checked-out repository files on disk at HEAD without .git metadata (1.42 MiB). Canopy fundamentally restructures repository hydration: canopy mount transfers only a lightweight 767-byte root manifest slice, expanding directory slices (e.g. apps/web/src) and streaming individual file blobs strictly on demand with local content-addressed deduplication.

📊 Benchmark Reproduction & PRNG Technical Detail

The benchmark suite generates a deterministic synthetic monorepo using a Mulberry32 PRNG (seed: 1337). All benchmark iterations are committed as machine-verifiable artifacts in docs/benchmark-results.json and audited on every run via npm run check-claims.

What Went Wrong & Lessons Learned

Engineering software that bridges low-level git internals, embedded databases, and probabilistic AI models invariably uncovers sharp edges. Here are four real problems we hit and how we solved them:

1. The Native SQLite Dilemma on Windows vs Linux (D007)

We wanted SQLite in WAL mode for synchronous, zero-network caching. In production Docker containers on Linux, better-sqlite3 compiled cleanly. But on developer Windows machines without Visual Studio C++ build tools installed, npm install choked on node-gyp.

  • The Fix: We architected a dual-engine database adapter (src/db/index.ts). It dynamically detects the runtime: on Node >= 22.5.0, it leverages Node's built-in node:sqlite (DatabaseSync), while falling back to better-sqlite3 when available. Both implement an identical TypeScript contract with zero API divergence.

🔧 Technical Detail: Dual SQLite Engine Adapter

// Dynamically selects node:sqlite or better-sqlite3 with standard WAL PRAGMAs
export function createDatabaseAdapter(dbPath: string): DatabaseAdapter {
  try {
    const { DatabaseSync } = require('node:sqlite');
    const db = new DatabaseSync(dbPath);
    db.exec('PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL; PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;');
    return new NodeSqliteAdapter(db);
  } catch {
    const Database = require('better-sqlite3');
    const db = new Database(dbPath);
    db.pragma('journal_mode = WAL');
    db.pragma('busy_timeout = 5000');
    return new BetterSqliteAdapter(db);
  }
}

2. The Platform-Locked Rollup Dependency Trap (D023)

While testing Docker builds, npm ci on Debian Linux crashed with EBADPLATFORM: Unsupported platform for @rollup/rollup-win32-x64-msvc. Running npm install on a Windows host had written Windows-specific optional native packages into package-lock.json.

  • The Fix: We cleaned platform-locked devDependencies from package.json, pinned engines.node to >=22.5.0, and updated our multi-stage Docker build to execute npm prune --omit=dev.

3. Ephemeral Port Clashing Behind Reverse Proxies (D024)

We implemented per-IP rate limiting (60 req/min) to safeguard our Google AI Studio demo quota. In local testing, bursts returned HTTP 429 cleanly. But when deployed behind Render and Cloudflare, requests intermittently bypassed rate limits.

  • The Investigation: Cloudflare and Render append proxy addresses to x-forwarded-for and attach ephemeral client ports (203.0.113.195:54321, :54322). Because each HTTP connection used a different ephemeral port, our IP map treated them as separate clients!
  • The Fix: We overhauled src/server/app.ts to prioritize cf-connecting-ip, split multi-hop x-forwarded-for headers, and strip trailing :port suffixes before looking up rate limits.

4. Production Cold Starts: Model Bakeoff & Thought Token Stripping (Measured Before/After)

Generating deep architectural digests requires significant LLM inference. During initial live deployment testing, cold inference latency was a serious barrier:

  • Measured Before: First-user cold digest latency took 13,705 ms p50 on Google AI Studio's Gemma 26B (models/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it), while Gemma 31B spiked to 24,200 ms p50 and hit a 116-second timeout with a degraded fallback. Furthermore, reasoning thought tokens enclosed in <thought>...</thought> blocks caused schema validation failures.
  • The Fix: We evaluated 26B vs 31B across 5 live runs each (scripts/bakeoff.ts, documented in docs/bakeoff.md). 26B achieved 100% first-try schema validity vs 80% for 31B. We patched DerivedService with regex thought stripping (<(thought|think)>[\s\S]*?<\/\1>), and implemented a background cache warmer (src/server/warmer.ts) pre-populating English & Bengali digests and 3 key architecture files on boot.
  • Measured After: First-user digest requests now hit SQLite cache in ~4 ms instead of ~13.7s (a 3,400x speedup), backed by 60s server timeouts and a visible warming status badge in the Web UI.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Code is proprietary, developer bandwidth is scarce, and infrastructure is expensive. The open-source AI paradigm offers distinct advantages:

  1. Vendor Sovereignty & Zero Lock-In: Canopy's LLM layer is built strictly on the standard OpenAI-compatible API format (/v1/chat/completions) without proprietary vendor SDKs. You can run Canopy against Google AI Studio's Gemma endpoint in the cloud, or point CANOPY_LLM_BASE_URL to a local Ollama instance (http://localhost:11434/v1) running on your laptop with zero code modifications.
  2. Offline Resilience: When internet access drops or API quotas are exhausted, Canopy doesn't crash. Every operation is guarded by strict Zod schemas, 2 automatic retries, and deterministic offline heuristic fallbacks flagged is_degraded = 1.
  3. Local Privacy: With local models via Ollama, zero lines of code or commit diffs ever leave your developer machine.

Honest Verification Status: Google AI Studio's hosted Gemma 4 model was fully verified live in production. The offline local path via Ollama is fully implemented with automated probing (npm run verify:ollama generating docs/ollama-results.json), but is currently marked unverified because the local Ollama daemon was not running on the Windows test machine during this build pass.

Sentry GenAI Agent Tracing & Privacy

Observability is essential when managing multi-agent AI systems. We integrated Sentry OpenTelemetry GenAI agent tracing across four designated agent personas:

  • CanopyDigestAgent: Commit range synthesis and risk assessment
  • CanopyWhyAgent: Architectural role and code evolution analysis
  • CanopyCommitAgent: Conventional commit message generation
  • CanopySummaryAgent: File-level responsibility extraction

Each span captures standard semantic attributes (gen_ai.system, gen_ai.request.model, prompt/completion tokens, input/output tokens, latency, cache hit/miss, retry count, and degraded status).

Privacy by Design

Developer code must remain confidential. In src/server/sentry.ts, we implemented strict privacy protections:

  • Client IP addresses are scrubbed and never stored (user.ip_address: undefined).
  • Raw diff payloads and file source contents are stripped from event context before envelope dispatch.

Run our automated trace demo generator to simulate and dispatch 20 real-world scenarios to Sentry:

npm run trace:demo

Note on Delivery Verification: Because client envelope dispatch is asynchronous fire-and-forget, traces must be visually confirmed by a human checking Explore > Agents in the Sentry dashboard.

My Agent Session

This project was built pair-programming with Antigravity, Google's agentic AI assistant.

Hackathon challenge eligibility and tracking were verified through the DevRelay MCP Gateway:

  • We called devrelay-gateway/get_challenges via MCP, confirming that Challenge ID 81 (Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 3: Slow and Steady) is ACTIVE through 2026-10-25T06:59:00Z (see DEVRELAY_STATUS.md).

Working with an agent was a rigorous pair-programming dialogue:

  • Diagnosing why Windows PowerShell requires ; instead of && for command chaining.
  • Inspecting Vitest logs when file extension heuristics generated .tsx instead of .ts.
  • Writing automated verification scripts (scripts/verify.ts) to validate every gate before committing.
  • Establishing an honest engineering standard: every single claim in this post and the repository README is verified by scripts/check-claims.ts against docs/benchmark-results.json.

🧪 Automated 7-Gate Verification Suite

Every release passes 7 sequential verification gates:

npm run verify
  1. Vitest suite (48 tests across 6 test suites)
  2. Local Mock LLM server startup
  3. Synthetic bare monorepo generation (3,000 files, 200 commits)
  4. Canopy server boot with SQLite WAL
  5. E2E lazy fetch benchmark (verifying >= 98% bandwidth savings)
  6. Zero-call cache hit assertion & bad-model 2-retry heuristic degradation
  7. Numerical claims audit against docs/benchmark-results.json

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma ($200): Canopy leverages Google Gemma 4 (models/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it) via Google AI Studio's OpenAI-compatible endpoint as its primary reasoning engine for structured file summaries, bilingual git digests, and architectural role explanations backed by thought token stripping, Zod schema validation, a 2-retry repair loop, and boot-time cache warming (src/server/derived.ts).
  • Best Use of Render ($200): Canopy is containerized with a production multi-stage Dockerfile and deployed on Render as an auto-seeding Web Service featuring an Infrastructure-as-Code Blueprint, automated REST API deployment orchestration, /healthz health monitoring, and proxy-aware per-IP rate limiting (render.yaml).
  • Best Use of Sentry ($200): Canopy instruments every LLM call across four designated agent personas following OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions with zero-leak IP and diff scrubbing, verifiable in Sentry under Explore > Agents (src/server/sentry.ts).
  • Best Use of GitHub ($200): Canopy integrates automated GitHub Actions CI verification gates, a 10-minute production keepwarm cron, repository Copilot guidance, a PR template, and curated good first issues with explicit acceptance criteria (.github/workflows/ci.yml).

articles.title: Crawlable Links in JavaScript Apps: Audit the Destination Behind the Click
articles.description: For public navigation in a JavaScript app, render a real link with an actual destination URL. A card...
articles.body_html:
For public navigation in a JavaScript app, render a real link with an actual destination URL. A card that opens the right page when clicked can still be a weak discovery path if its address exists only inside a click handler. Audit the link element and the destination separately: one exposes the route, while the other must deliver the promised page.

This is a practical crawlable-links check for product pages, documentation and comparison guides. It is also useful groundwork for AI search optimization, without proving that any answer engine will discover, cite or recommend the page. The review below is a proposed procedure with hypothetical examples, not a report of tests on a live site.

Start with the rendered link

Google's link best practices generally call for an HTML anchor element with an href attribute. Google says it cannot reliably extract destinations from anchors without href or from other elements that act as links through script events. It also permits dynamically inserted links when they use the recommended markup.

That distinction keeps the review focused. JavaScript is not automatically the problem. The important question is whether the rendered control exposes a resolvable address. A library component named Link might produce a suitable anchor, while a component with an ordinary-looking card might produce only a div. Inspect the output rather than guessing from its name.

A route that appears in your sitemap does not answer this particular question. The sitemap may provide a separate discovery route, but it does not turn the visible card into a useful link. Record which path you are testing so that an alternate source of discovery does not hide the defect.

Separate navigation from an action

Begin with the user's intended result. Opening a public guide, product page or comparison is navigation. Saving a preference, submitting a form or expanding an explanation is an action. Some interfaces combine them, so inspect each responsibility before choosing the element.

In a hypothetical documentation library, a card titled Import contacts should lead to the public import guide. The destination belongs in a link. A filter called CSV might instead change which cards appear on the current page. That control needs to operate as an action unless the design intentionally gives the filtered view its own public destination.

A menu can contain both. Its trigger opens the menu, while its entries navigate to documents. Making the trigger a button does not mean the entries should be buttons too. Review the controls at the point where their job changes, especially when a shared component is reused across several templates.

Audit three ordinary interface patterns

Consider a fictional SaaS help center with topic cards, search results and a product menu. The topic cards contain descriptive titles but rely on an onClick handler to call the router. Search results render anchors with valid href values. Product-menu entries look like links but use a JavaScript expression as their destination.

The first pattern needs an exposed address for each public destination. The second already passes the markup part of the check, although its routes still need direct-load testing. The third requires a real URL in place of the expression. These are three different findings, even if all controls work during a normal clicking session.

Now inspect a card that contains a secondary Bookmark button. Do not solve the navigation issue by making every nested control part of one click target. Preserve the separate jobs: the title link opens the guide, while the button changes the saved state. Review keyboard behavior as part of the interaction check, without treating keyboard access as proof of crawler discovery.

Use five checks for each public destination

First, inspect the rendered element. Confirm that the actual navigation link is an anchor with href, rather than a similarly styled span or an address stored only in component state. Record the page template and exact control so another developer can locate the finding.

Second, read the href value. It should resolve to the intended public page. An empty value, placeholder hash or JavaScript expression needs investigation. A section anchor within an existing document has a different purpose from a link to another document; do not change valid section navigation merely because it contains a hash.

Third, copy the destination and open it directly in a fresh tab. Verify the expected title, answer and access state. If direct arrival fails but clicking through the app succeeds, the link and route checks have found separate issues. Repairing the anchor alone cannot fix the server response or a missing public route.

Fourth, inspect the rendered text. Does the link describe the destination accurately? Fifth, check that a relevant public page actually includes the link. A technically correct component sitting behind a private dashboard is not the same discovery path as a public help-center link.

Keep client-side navigation without hiding the address

Client-side routing and real links can coexist. Your router may intercept ordinary navigation to update the interface efficiently while preserving a usable href in the rendered anchor. Check the router's current official guidance before changing its component behavior; this article does not assume every framework uses the same API.

Review the result after rendering, including any delayed data load. A correct anchor in a component file is not enough if the deployed page replaces it with another control, strips its href or never renders the relevant cards. Likewise, an initial response without the link is not proof that JavaScript can never expose it.

For important public navigation, reduce avoidable dependence on interaction before the link exists. That is an engineering recommendation about making the path easier to inspect and use. It is not a promise about how quickly a crawler will render the page or whether a particular AI product executes the same scripts.

Make the destination promise readable

Google's guidance recommends descriptive, reasonably concise anchor text with useful surrounding context. Apply that to the actual reader task. Read the CSV field requirements sets a clearer expectation than Learn more when the destination is a field-format reference.

Avoid turning every anchor into a long keyword list. The reader needs to understand the next page, not your entire search strategy. On a card with an image, title and description, inspect which element provides the link text and whether the surrounding wording still makes the destination clear.

A mismatch can be editorial rather than technical. If a link promises supported imports but leads to a generic sales page, the markup may pass while the reader's question remains unanswered. Record that finding separately so the content team can fix the promise or provide a better destination.

Verify the repair at the template level

After changing a shared card or menu component, sample the templates that use it. Include a normal page, an empty result state, a translated page if relevant and a destination with special characters. Choose cases from the actual system rather than collecting a large number of identical screenshots.

For each sample, retain the source page, rendered element, resolved destination and direct-arrival result. Note authentication and device conditions that change the interface. The purpose is a small, repeatable acceptance record, not a claim that one sample establishes site-wide correctness.

Google's generative AI search guidance keeps foundational SEO relevant to its AI features. A crawlable link is part of that foundation, but discovery, indexing, answer inclusion and conversion remain separate outcomes. Check each with its own evidence instead of calling a repaired click handler an AI visibility gain.

Choose one public card grid today and follow a single important destination from rendered anchor to direct arrival. If either part fails, you have a concrete issue to fix and a clear way to verify the repair. Expand the audit only when another template or failure pattern gives you a reason.
