articles.title: Feature Flag Testing: Make Your Public Demo's Access Boundary Clear
articles.description: When you share a public demo of a feature behind a flag, state which environment and kind of account...
articles.body_html:
When you share a public demo of a feature behind a flag, state which environment and kind of account received the feature, what variation was enabled, and what you actually observed working. Then explain what an ordinary visitor can do today. A successful recording of a selected test account does not establish general availability.

For developers building in public, this is both a testing problem and a communication problem. The feature may be real while the access described by the post is misleading. A useful demo keeps its setup visible enough for a founder peer to understand the result, without exposing credentials, private identifiers or customer data.

Define the claim before you record the feature

Consider a fictional SaaS tool that groups imported support requests. Its founder has added a suggested category panel behind a feature flag. The next public update should show how that panel works and invite feedback on the category explanation. It should not imply that every customer already has the feature.

Write the intended claim first: a selected demo account can see and review category suggestions in the current preview build. That describes a bounded capability. Keep a separate sentence for availability: other accounts still see the existing manual categorization flow.

These statements answer different reader questions. The first explains the work being demonstrated. The second explains what someone arriving from the post should expect. If either statement is uncertain, verify it before publishing the recording or narrow the post accordingly.

Record the setup without publishing the secrets

Keep a private record of the application version, environment, test identity category, relevant flag variation and fixture data used for the recording. The public version usually needs a smaller description: preview environment, a test account explicitly included in the rollout, and fictional support requests.

Do not display an SDK key, targeting identifier, account email or a configuration page containing unrelated users. Showing that a flag exists is rarely the useful part of the product story. Show the reader the behavior and explain the relevant access boundary in plain words.

LaunchDarkly's testing guidance describes targeting as a way to serve variations to particular contexts. It also distinguishes fallback values used when evaluation cannot complete. Those are useful concepts for planning the demo, regardless of which flag system your product uses. They do not replace checking the application itself.

Check the selected experience and the ordinary experience

For the fictional support tool, first open the selected demo account and complete the intended task with fictional requests. Confirm that the suggested category appears, that its explanation is readable and that accepting it changes the request as expected. Record what happens after saving and reopening the item.

Then inspect an account that is outside the preview. Verify that it receives the intended existing workflow and that the public link does not promise access it cannot provide. A label saying preview is not enough if the page invites everyone to use a control that only selected accounts can see.

Keep these observations separate in your notes. A configured on state is evidence of configuration. Seeing a panel is evidence that it rendered. Saving a chosen category and reopening it is evidence about that specific journey. None alone proves that every account or every data shape behaves correctly.

Choose a small set of meaningful flag states

Do not turn a public demo into an attempt to exhaust every possible flag combination. Choose the states that matter to the current claim and known risks. For this example, those include the selected preview experience, the ordinary off experience and the intended fallback when evaluation is unavailable.

LaunchDarkly recommends a defined set of test scenarios, including current and upcoming production settings, fallback values and important problematic states. Apply that principle deliberately. The article's suggested checks are a focused demonstration plan, not a complete test strategy for every application.

If another flag controls a prerequisite, include it in the setup record. A category panel might depend on a particular import format or permission. Demonstrating one flag without noting that dependency could leave a peer unable to understand why their otherwise similar account shows something different.

Test fallback through your normal supported process

A fallback state is not just another screenshot. You need to understand which behavior the application serves if flag evaluation cannot complete. Use the supported test facilities and established environment for your system. Do not disrupt real customers or weaken access controls to produce a dramatic public example.

For the fictional product, the intended fallback might be manual categorization. The useful check is whether a tester can still complete that supported task and whether the interface explains the available route. If the application instead blocks the whole request list, the public update should not describe fallback as harmless.

Document the difference between a deliberately configured off variation and an evaluation failure. They may lead to the same visible result while exercising different paths. If you have only checked the off state, say that. Do not label an untested failure mode as verified recovery.

Make the demo explain its own availability

Put the access boundary close to the demonstration, where a reader can encounter it without opening another thread. A suitable hypothetical caption is: “This is the category preview in a selected test account. General accounts still use manual categories. The requests shown are fictional.”

Avoid a headline such as “Category suggestions are live” if the post never explains the restricted rollout. A more accurate title could name the preview and the question being reviewed. Specific wording lets you share real progress without converting a controlled test into a general launch announcement.

I build Buildside. Its public product description includes founders sharing progress and finding concrete help. A demo with a clear boundary gives peers useful context for feedback. It does not imply that Buildside tested your implementation or that a community response certifies the feature.

Ask peers about the part they can actually assess

The founder in this example wants feedback on the category explanation. Give a peer one fictional request, the suggested category and its stated reason. Ask what they think the suggestion means and what information they would need before accepting it. Keep that question distinct from whether they would buy the whole product.

If the peer cannot access the preview, provide an accurate recording or a safe test route you are authorized to share. Do not ask them to borrow another person's account. A reviewer watching a recording can assess what is communicated; they cannot verify an interaction they have not performed.

Record the review method beside the response. “Watched the recording” and “completed the task in the preview account” describe different evidence. That small distinction helps prevent a public discussion about wording from becoming an unsupported claim that the workflow has been validated.

Recheck the post when the rollout changes

After recording, compare the published caption and destination with the current rollout. If the feature opens to more accounts, update the availability statement where practical. If the preview closes, make the old post's status clear so a new visitor does not mistake historical access for a current invitation.

Keep the original observation honest. A later rollout does not retroactively prove the earlier demo covered all users. Likewise, a later bug does not mean the recorded test never worked. Date the evidence and describe which setup produced it.

For the fictional support tool, the finished update can show the selected journey, state the ordinary experience, name the review question and acknowledge what remains untested. That is enough to make the work understandable. The reader sees a feature in a defined state, and the developer keeps a useful record of what was actually checked.

articles.title: 5 Steps on How to not loose at a hackathon?
articles.description: In 1999, ten developers gathered to work on cryptographic frameworks, IPv6, and IPsec for OpenBSD, in...
articles.body_html:
In 1999, ten developers gathered to work on cryptographic frameworks, IPv6, and IPsec for OpenBSD, in what is often considered the first-ever hackathon. Since then, the tech world has decided that the best way to encourage innovation is to put a few hundred developers in a building, deprive them of sleep, give them unlimited caffeine, and ask them to build something extraordinary in 24 to 48 hours.

Rather surprisingly, it worked.

Hackathons have become places where people build remarkable projects, discover new technologies, make lifelong friends, and occasionally spend six hours debugging something that could have been fixed by restarting their computer.

I started participating in hackathons in my first year of college, eventually began organizing them, and today, as a Hackathon Community Manager at Major League Hacking (@mlhacks), I work with organizers and hackers across the community. Along the way, I've noticed something: some people walk away with incredible experiences but no trophies, while others spend the whole weekend obsessing over winning and miss everything else that makes hackathons worthwhile.

So, how exactly does one avoid losing at a hackathon? Here are five steps. They won't guarantee a prize, although my definition of winning might be slightly different from yours.

Step 1: Talk to People. A Radical Concept, I Know.

You arrive surrounded by hundreds of people who share your interest in building things. Naturally, the sensible move is to find a corner, put on your headphones, and avoid all of them for 36 hours.

Or perhaps not.

Hackathons bring together developers exploring new frameworks, designers who approach problems differently, first-timers discovering what an API is, and veterans who've already made every mistake you're about to make. Talk to them. Ask what they're building and why. You don't need a networking strategy; a simple conversation is usually enough.

Talk to the organizers too. They've spent months on an event you're experiencing over a weekend. And at MLH-supported events, talk to the MLH reps. We're not just there to explain rules and hand out stickers (though stickers are an extremely compelling reason to approach anyone btw). We can connect you with resources, opportunities, and people worth knowing.

You might come looking for a teammate and leave with a mentor, a future collaborator, or someone who shares your inexplicably specific interest in apps for household appliances. You won't find any of them by staring at your terminal.

Step 2: Observe. There's a Lot Happening Beyond Your Screen.

In one corner, someone's building an AI app. Across the room, a team is assembling hardware with a worrying number of exposed wires. Somewhere else, a group has just discovered that the technology they spent twelve hours integrating doesn't support the one feature their project depends on.

Watch how other teams divide work, which tools they try, and how they decide what to do when something breaks. Most importantly, pay attention to how they think. One team might build a complicated ML pipeline while another solves the same problem with simple software and clever design. Neither is automatically better, and understanding why someone chose a solution is often worth more than the solution itself.

(No, this isn't an invitation to copy someone's project or acquire their GitHub repo through questionable means.)

Walk around and attend demos. Hackathons pack enormous amounts of knowledge into small spaces, and it would be a shame to spend the weekend accessing only what's already on your laptop.

Step 3: Ask Questions. Particularly the Ones You Think Are Stupid.

There's a peculiar belief among developers that everyone else knows exactly what they're doing. They don't. Some are just better at maintaining the appearance.

Hackathons give you mentors, workshops, and experienced developers who are all there to help people build things. Use them. If you're stuck, ask. If a workshop covers something unfamiliar, ask. There's no noble reason to spend four hours debugging something someone could explain in ten minutes.

Figuring things out yourself is valuable, and getting thoroughly confused is practically a tradition in software development. But knowing when to ask for help is a skill too. And sometimes the best question isn't "How do I do this?" but "Why did you build it this way?"

Step 4: Build Something Great. Whatever That Means.

Ah, yes. The actual project. You may have noticed we're only getting to it at Step 4. This is intentional.

We've developed strange expectations about what makes a project great. Apparently it must revolutionize education, transform healthcare, end climate change, or use AI to fix an inconvenience humanity has tolerated for centuries. Preferably within 24 hours.

Solving meaningful problems is worthwhile, but not every great hackathon project needs to save the world. Sometimes it solves a small problem exceptionally well, combines existing tools in an interesting way, or, especially for beginners, is simply something you've always wanted to build.

Start with something that interests you. Great ideas often begin with "Wouldn't it be interesting if I could build something that does this?" Maybe that's computer vision, language models on physical hardware, a tool for an annoying task, or just a fun game. When you care about the idea, you'll keep going when something inevitably breaks. And something will inevitably break.

Experiment with technology. Don't just collect it. Hackathons are a great place to try unfamiliar APIs, frameworks, and hardware. But integrating a tool because it improves your project is different from integrating it because its logo looks good on a slide or MLH is giving out a prize for it. Good technical decisions aren't about using the most tools; they're about choosing the right ones.

Step 5: Collect Feedback, Not Just Stickers.

Let me be clear: stickers are important. I've been in the hackathon space for over three years, I work at MLH, and I'm obsessed with a good sticker collection.

But you should also collect feedback.

One of the biggest mistakes is guarding your project like a state secret until judging, only to discover that the feature you spent ten hours perfecting isn't useful to anyone but you. An unfortunate discovery to make three minutes before judging ends.

Share early. Explain your idea to another team, run your approach past a mentor, and show someone a prototype to see if they get it without a fifteen-minute explanation. If they don't, or they suggest something simpler, or they spot a problem you missed, that's all useful information.

And if another team is stuck on something you've solved before, help them. You're not giving away your chances of winning. Hackathons are competitions, but they're also communities, and the two can coexist just fine.

So, Did You Win?

At the end, the judges decide. Some teams win prizes. Most go home without a trophy, presumably after locating their chargers and remembering what uninterrupted sleep feels like.

But consider what you've gained. You met people you wouldn't otherwise have met, explored new technologies, and built something that didn't exist when you arrived. Maybe it worked perfectly. Maybe it worked only during the demo, an achievement deserving its own category of engineering recognition. Or maybe it didn't work at all, but now you know why and what you'd do differently.

Winning a prize is wonderful, so work hard and give the judges every reason to recognize you. Just don't make it the only measure of whether your weekend was worthwhile.

A hackathon is one of those rare competitions where you can lose the judging round and still leave with more than you arrived with.

And if you've managed that, I'd argue you've followed these five steps rather successfully.

MLH Hackathons are the best place to lean, connect and grow in the tech space. So, at your next MLH Hackathon, don't forget to follow the 5 steps and don't forget to grab some awesome stickers and swag!

articles.title: Most Package Managers Won't Stop a Tampered Download by Default
articles.description: Trail of Bits tested 25 package managers against a compromised server. Only Go and vcpkg verified every download. Here's what to change in your CI.
articles.body_html:
Keegan Ryan of the security firm Trail of Bits set up a fake compromised package server and pointed 25 popular package managers at it. Two of them, Go and vcpkg, verified every package they downloaded, even without a lockfile. Without one, the other 23 installed whatever they were given.

Lockfiles didn't rescue most of them either.

The test

Ryan routed each tool's traffic through a proxy that could rewrite downloads, then installed quickstart projects with default settings, with and without a lockfile. An attack counted as a success if the injected code ran. The threat model assumes any web-facing server, such as a registry or a mirror, can be compromised, but backend secrets like private signing keys can't.

The lockfile is the safety net, and it's mostly unplugged

A lockfile pins every dependency's exact version and, ideally, a hash: a fingerprint the download has to match. Fewer than half of the 25 tools checked those hashes by default.

All 25 package managers, by default behavior. Source: Trail of Bits, October 14, 2026.

Nine verify when a lockfile is present, including npm, pnpm, Cargo, uv and Yarn. Five can verify, but only with extra steps. The last nine don't verify lockfile hashes at all, or the check doesn't apply to them.

Checks that don't stop anything

Tools with no check are the obvious failures. The sneakier ones run a check and install anyway:

  • Pub (Dart and Flutter) detects a hash mismatch, installs the package anyway and updates the lockfile to match, unless you pass --enforce-lockfile. Some Flutter commands run pub get too, and can overwrite the lockfile unless called with --no-pub.
  • pnpm overwrote the lockfile on a mismatch until version 11.4, in May 2026, so the tampered package simply became the new truth.
  • Composer (PHP) locks a Git commit, then downloads a ZIP archive it never checks against that commit.
  • CocoaPods hashes the package spec but fetches the source by Git tag, which a compromised host could serve with different contents.
  • cpanminus (Perl) still connects to its repository over plain HTTP by default.

Four outcomes when the download and the lockfile disagree. Only the green one protects you.

Why the defaults are like this

None of this is hidden; it's documented behavior. Lockfiles were built for reproducible installs, and as Ryan notes, reading them through a supply-chain lens "is a recent interpretation that can be at odds with their original design." Strict pinning also has a cost: every update, security fixes included, needs a lockfile change.

Go shows the alternative. It checks every hash against a signed checksum database that works like a transparency log, which makes targeted tampering much harder, at the cost of concentrating trust in a single private key. It was the only tool that verified every download and checked signatures by default. As Ryan puts it, "Package signing is in a similar state now to where HTTPS was a decade ago."

What to do this week

  1. Commit your lockfile, at least for applications. Norms for libraries vary by ecosystem.
  2. Install in strict mode in CI: npm ci, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, uv sync --locked, pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt (with hashes generated by pip-compile --generate-hashes) or dart pub get --enforce-lockfile.
  3. If your tool needs extra steps, take them: the conda-lock library for Conda, a verification-metadata.xml file for Gradle, the RestorePackagesWithLockFile property for NuGet.
  4. If your tool is in the last group, don't treat its lockfile as a security control. Maven can check signatures against trusted keys with the third-party pgpverify-maven-plugin. Beyond that, the fallback Conan's developers suggest applies widely: if integrity is critical, run your own repository server.

Then test it: change one hash in your lockfile on purpose and confirm CI fails.

Caveats

Each tool was tested with one package, one version and one platform, Ubuntu, and some setups, like PowerShell and CocoaPods on Ubuntu, don't reflect typical use. The study shows that reasonable defaults can leave you exposed, not that every setup is.

Verification comes before detection

Most supply chain tooling hunts for packages already known to be bad. This study is about the step before that: making sure the package you got is the package you asked for. For most of the 25 tools, that check is off by default or missing. Where it exists, turning it on is about the cheapest security win you'll find.

If you check what your package manager does on a hash mismatch, I'd like to hear what you find.

Sources

  • Package managers have an integrity problem, Keegan Ryan, Trail of Bits, October 14, 2026

articles.body_html:
Today we celebrate the official release of version 2.0 of the MiniScript programming language!

Download MiniScript 2 here!

This is a complete rewrite, from the ground up, focused primarily on performance. The results do not disappoint: MiniScript 2 clocks in at 45X - 50X faster on some benchmarks, with an average of 10X - 15X faster across the board.

It also brings some cool language improvements, including:

  • Better error handling
  • Frozen lists and maps
  • Computed lists
  • Mark-and-sweep garbage collection, even in C++

Today's release includes a new & improved command-line build for Linux, Windows, Mac, and any .NET platform. This can be used interactively, with a powerful REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) that lets you reference earlier inputs and outputs; or it can be used to create scripts and programs to run from the command line. Those can include sophisticated terminal control, enabling interactive text user interfaces like this:

That's one of the examples included with the download; another one is a modern port of the classic "Super Star Trek" game:

But MiniScript 2 is not just for fun and games! The command-line environment includes full support for manipulating files and data, both text-based and binary; executing shell commands; reading the shell arguments; parsing JSON data; and more. articles.title: I Allocated 1.5 GB Just to Add Vectors Together
articles.description: C# 14 lets you write your own in-place +=. I used it to fold 200,000 vectors with zero allocations instead of 1.5 GB, and measured the gap.
articles.body_html:
I had a loop that did something embarrassingly simple: fold a stream of feature vectors into one running total. Add a vector, add the next, keep going. A few hundred thousand of them. The math is a for-loop over some doubles, nothing that should trouble the garbage collector.

The allocation profile said otherwise. Gigabytes. For adding numbers.

I knew why the second I looked at the operator. I'd written + the tidy, immutable way years ago and never thought about it again:

public static Vec operator +(Vec a, Vec b)
{
    var result = new double[a.Data.Length];
    for (int i = 0; i < result.Length; i++)
        result[i] = a.Data[i] + b.Data[i];
    return new Vec(result);
}

That's a perfectly reasonable operator. Every call hands back a brand new Vec with its own fresh array, nobody's state gets stomped, and you can reason about it without fear. It's also a fresh 8 KB array on the heap every single time you add two 1024-dimension vectors. In a one-off expression that's free. In a fold over a stream, it's a steady firehose into gen 0.

My accumulation loop was the firehose:

var acc = new Vec(Dims);
for (int i = 0; i < input.Length; i++)
    acc = acc + input[i];

Read that acc = acc + input[i] again. I'm allocating a whole new accumulator on every iteration and throwing the old one away. I never needed a new object. I wanted to pour the next vector into the one I already had.

The operator I couldn't write before

Until C# 14 there was no clean way to say that. += was always just sugar for a = a + b: it called your operator +, took the result, and assigned it back. You couldn't hook the "in place" part because there was no in-place part to hook.

C# 14 adds user-defined compound assignment operators. You write operator += as its own thing. It's an instance method, it returns void, and it mutates this.

public void operator +=(Vec other)
{
    var mine = Data;
    var theirs = other.Data;
    for (int i = 0; i < mine.Length; i++)
        mine[i] += theirs[i];
}

No new. No array. It reaches into the buffer this instance already owns and adds the other vector straight into it. The call site doesn't change at all: acc += input[i] now finds this operator instead of falling back to +. If I hadn't written it, the compiler would've quietly used operator + like always. You only get the new behavior when you opt in.

I counted it

I don't trust "should be faster," so I measured. I built 200,000 vectors of 1024 doubles each, folded them both ways, and tracked wall-clock time (best of five) alongside bytes allocated with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread(). This is a container with workstation GC, not a lab bench, so I care about the ratio and the allocation column, not the exact milliseconds.

dims=1024, vectors=200,000, rounds=5, GC=workstation

acc = acc + v   best    740.0 ms   allocated   1571.7 MB   checksum 102400896.09
acc += v        best    301.9 ms   allocated      0.0 MB   checksum 102400896.09

same result: True
time ratio:  2.45x

1.5 GB versus zero. Same checksum, so the two loops genuinely compute the same answer. The in-place version came out 2.45x faster, and most of that gap isn't the addition. It's the collector cleaning up a gigabyte and a half of short-lived arrays that never had any reason to exist. Zero megabytes still makes me grin a little. The whole fold runs without handing the GC a single byte.

When I'd leave the old operator alone

Here's the part the benchmark won't tell you: mutating in place throws away the one thing immutable + was buying you. With operator +, nobody's vector changes under them. With operator +=, if two references point at the same Vec and one of them does +=, the other just silently got mutated too. That's a classic aliasing bug, and it's exactly the kind of thing that's fine in a tight local loop and nasty in a shared domain model.

So I'm not about to replace every + with an in-place +=. For value-ish types you pass around, compare, and cache, immutability is worth more than the allocations. My honest rule: reach for the in-place operator when you've got a genuine hot accumulation loop and the accumulator is local and yours. Everywhere else, let + keep making new things.

One more sharp edge. The compiler doesn't enforce consistency, so you can define += without +, or make them disagree, and it won't say a word. I'd keep the two in sync regardless, because a += that quietly diverges from + is a debugging session waiting to happen.

I normally drop a link to the runnable sample here, but my code repo push got blocked this time, so the whole thing is right below. Target net10.0 with <LangVersion>14</LangVersion> and it runs as-is:

using System.Diagnostics;

sealed class Vec
{
    public readonly double[] Data;

    public Vec(int dims) => Data = new double[dims];
    public Vec(double[] data) => Data = data;

    // Immutable style: a fresh Vec + array on every add.
    public static Vec operator +(Vec a, Vec b)
    {
        var result = new double[a.Data.Length];
        for (int i = 0; i < result.Length; i++)
            result[i] = a.Data[i] + b.Data[i];
        return new Vec(result);
    }

    // C# 14 in-place compound assignment: mutates this buffer, allocates nothing.
    public void operator +=(Vec other)
    {
        var mine = Data;
        var theirs = other.Data;
        for (int i = 0; i < mine.Length; i++)
            mine[i] += theirs[i];
    }

    public double Checksum()
    {
        double s = 0;
        foreach (var d in Data) s += d;
        return s;
    }
}

static class Program
{
    const int Dims = 1024;
    const int Count = 200_000;
    const int Rounds = 5;

    static Vec[] BuildInputs()
    {
        var rng = new Random(42);
        var vecs = new Vec[Count];
        for (int i = 0; i < Count; i++)
        {
            var d = new double[Dims];
            for (int j = 0; j < Dims; j++) d[j] = rng.NextDouble();
            vecs[i] = new Vec(d);
        }
        return vecs;
    }

    static (double sum, long bytes, double ms) RunPlus(Vec[] input)
    {
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        var acc = new Vec(Dims);
        for (int i = 0; i < input.Length; i++)
            acc = acc + input[i];
        long after = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        sw.Stop();
        return (acc.Checksum(), after - before, sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
    }

    static (double sum, long bytes, double ms) RunCompound(Vec[] input)
    {
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        var acc = new Vec(Dims);
        for (int i = 0; i < input.Length; i++)
            acc += input[i];
        long after = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        sw.Stop();
        return (acc.Checksum(), after - before, sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
    }

    static void Main()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"dims={Dims}, vectors={Count:N0}, rounds={Rounds}, GC=workstation");
        var input = BuildInputs();

        _ = RunPlus(input);      // warm up the JIT
        _ = RunCompound(input);

        double plusChk = 0, compChk = 0, plusBest = double.MaxValue, compBest = double.MaxValue;
        long plusBytes = 0, compBytes = 0;

        for (int r = 0; r < Rounds; r++)
        {
            var p = RunPlus(input);
            var c = RunCompound(input);
            plusChk = p.sum; compChk = c.sum;
            plusBytes = p.bytes; compBytes = c.bytes;
            if (p.ms < plusBest) plusBest = p.ms;
            if (c.ms < compBest) compBest = c.ms;
        }

        Console.WriteLine($"acc = acc + v   best {plusBest,8:F1} ms   allocated {plusBytes / (1024.0 * 1024.0),8:F1} MB   checksum {plusChk:F2}");
        Console.WriteLine($"acc += v        best {compBest,8:F1} ms   allocated {compBytes / (1024.0 * 1024.0),8:F1} MB   checksum {compChk:F2}");
        Console.WriteLine($"same result: {Math.Abs(plusChk - compChk) < 1e-6}");
        Console.WriteLine($"time ratio:  {plusBest / compBest:F2}x");
    }
}

Have you hit a spot where += was quietly allocating behind your back? I'd like to hear where it bit you.

— still benchmarking things nobody asked me to benchmark

articles.title: Your AI Agent Says “Done.” What Did It Actually Verify?
articles.description: “Fixed the bug. All tests pass.”  Great.  Which tests? Did they run? Did they cover the bug—or did...
articles.body_html:
“Fixed the bug. All tests pass.”

Great.

Which tests? Did they run? Did they cover the bug—or did the agent change the test until it passed?

A confident completion message is easy to read as proof. But before you merge the changes, you need to understand what actually happened.

Here’s a simple workflow for checking an AI agent’s work without manually repeating every step.

1. Define “done” before it starts

“Fix the checkout bug” leaves too much open to interpretation.

Give the agent an observable outcome:

When a discount exceeds the order subtotal, the total should be zero. Add a regression test. Preserve valid discount behavior.

Now you have something concrete to verify.

For a UI task, describe the interaction. For an API task, specify the response and side effects.

Clear acceptance criteria make both implementation and verification easier.

2. Ask for evidence in the completion report

A useful report should include:

  • What changed.
  • Which commands ran.
  • Whether they passed or failed.
  • What could not be checked.

Compare these two reports:

“Everything works.”

And:

“Added a regression test for excessive discounts. The checkout test suite passed. Browser checkout was not tested because payment credentials were unavailable.”

The second report tells you what you can rely on and what still needs attention.

When your tool exposes execution logs, inspect them. A command mentioned in a summary is still a claim until you can confirm its execution.

3. Make sure the test catches the original bug

A passing test is useful only if it checks the behavior you care about.

Suppose the task is to prevent negative totals.

This assertion tells you almost nothing:

expect(result).toBeDefined();

This one checks the requirement:

expect(calculateTotal(50, 80)).toBe(0);

Where practical, confirm that the regression test fails against the original implementation and passes after the fix.

Then check nearby behavior:

expect(calculateTotal(50, 20)).toBe(30);

The goal is to demonstrate that the bug was fixed while preserving expected behavior.

4. Read changes to the tests themselves

Sometimes the implementation needs to change. Sometimes an outdated test needs to change too.

But a green result deserves closer inspection if the agent also:

  • Skipped a failing test.
  • Removed an important assertion.
  • Replaced realistic behavior with a convenient mock.
  • Changed the expected result to match the implementation.
  • Disabled a check in configuration.

These changes can have valid reasons. Ask for the reason and compare it with the requirement.

“Tests pass” has limited meaning if the relevant checks were weakened.

5. Match verification to the change

Different changes need different evidence.

Change Useful verification
Calculation Expected values and boundary cases
API endpoint Status, response body, permissions, and stored changes
Database migration Apply it to representative data and check compatibility
UI interaction Run the interaction and inspect the resulting state
Background job Check retries, duplicate handling, and failure behavior

A successful build proves that the build completed. It doesn’t prove that checkout works.

A screenshot shows appearance. It doesn’t prove that the button saves anything.

Choose checks that exercise the promised behavior.

6. Look for fixes that moved the problem

A small bug can lead to a surprisingly large patch.

Before merging, ask:

  • Did the agent change unrelated files?
  • Did it introduce a dependency for a small task?
  • Did it suppress an error instead of handling it?
  • Did it remove validation to make the request succeed?
  • Did it change a shared function and miss its other callers?

Start with the diff summary, then inspect the affected paths.

A large change isn’t automatically wrong. It should have an explanation proportional to its scope.

7. Treat blocked verification as unfinished verification

Sometimes the agent cannot run a check.

The database is unavailable. A dependency cannot be installed. Browser access is missing.

That is useful information.

The report should say:

“Implemented the change, but integration tests could not run because the test database was unavailable.”

Avoid turning “could not test” into “probably works.”

Record the missing check and complete it in the appropriate environment before relying on the result.

A prompt you can reuse

Add this to your next coding task:

Before editing, state the expected behavior and how you will verify it.

After editing, report:

  1. What changed.
  2. The exact checks you ran and their results.
  3. Whether the regression test catches the original failure, if applicable.
  4. Any tests or checks you changed, removed, or skipped—and why.
  5. What remains unverified.

Only claim a check passed if you actually ran it and observed a passing result.

This won’t eliminate mistakes. It gives you a clearer starting point for assessing the work.

Before you click merge

Ask one question:

“What evidence shows that this change meets the requirement?”

Sometimes the answer is a focused regression test. Sometimes it is an integration run, a browser interaction, or several checks together.

The important part is being able to connect the evidence to the task.

An AI agent can help you implement and verify a change. Its final message should make that verification inspectable.

What’s the biggest gap you’ve found between an agent saying “done” and the work actually being finished?

articles.description: Advanced RAG Architecture   A deep-dive walkthrough of production-grade Retrieval-Augmented...
articles.body_html:
Advanced RAG Architecture

A deep-dive walkthrough of production-grade Retrieval-Augmented Generation in .NET — covering document ingestion pipelines, PDF/Word/Excel/HTML parsing, OCR for scanned documents, semantic chunking and overlap strategies, parent-child retrieval, hierarchical indexing, query rewriting and expansion, hybrid search with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, cross-encoder reranking, metadata filtering, context compression, GraphRAG, agentic RAG, corrective RAG, RAG caching, and benchmarking — with C# code for every technique and guidance on when each one is worth its cost.

Table of Contents

  1. Introduction
  2. Document Ingestion Pipelines
  3. Parsing PDF, Word, Excel, and HTML
  4. OCR for Scanned Documents
  5. Semantic Chunking
  6. Chunk Overlap Strategies
  7. Parent-Child Retrieval
  8. Hierarchical Indexing
  9. Query Rewriting
  10. Query Expansion
  11. Hybrid Search (Keyword + Vector)
  12. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
  13. Cross-Encoder Reranking
  14. Metadata Filtering
  15. Context Compression
  16. GraphRAG
  17. Agentic RAG
  18. Corrective RAG
  19. RAG Caching
  20. RAG Benchmarking
  21. Putting It Together
  22. Common Pitfalls
  23. Quick Reference Table
  24. Conclusion

Introduction

The first RAG guide in this series built the baseline: extract text, chunk it, embed it, retrieve the top-k, put it in a prompt, and validate the answer. That baseline works surprisingly well on simple questions over clean documents — and then plateaus. Real corpora are messy (scanned PDFs, tables, spreadsheets, web pages with navigation junk), real questions are vague, multi-part, or conversational, and real requirements include access control, freshness, cost, and latency budgets. Advanced RAG is the set of techniques that close those gaps, each aimed at a specific, diagnosable failure.

BASELINE:   documents -> chunk -> embed -> top-k vector search -> prompt -> answer

ADVANCED:
  INGESTION    sources -> change detection -> PARSE (PDF/Word/Excel/HTML) -> OCR where needed -> clean/enrich -> STRUCTURE-AWARE/SEMANTIC CHUNKS
               (+ parent/child, summaries, graph extraction) -> embed -> index (vector + keyword + metadata)
  QUERY        question -> REWRITE / EXPAND -> HYBRID retrieval (keyword + vector, filtered) -> RRF fusion -> RERANK -> expand to parents/neighbors
               -> COMPRESS -> grounded generation -> VALIDATE -> (CORRECT and retry when evidence is weak)
  AROUND IT    caching · benchmarking · observability · security

The organizing rule of this guide: diagnose before you add. Every technique has a cost (latency, tokens, ingestion spend, complexity), and several give small or inconsistent gains on some corpora. Section 19 (benchmarking) is therefore not an appendix — it is the mechanism that tells you which of the other nineteen sections your system actually needs. Build the baseline, measure where it fails, add one technique, re-measure.

This guide builds directly on RAG, Embeddings & Vector Search, LLM Application Development, AI Agents, AI Security, AI Observability, and Microsoft.Extensions.AI, and avoids repeating them. Code uses Microsoft.Extensions.AI (IChatClient, IEmbeddingGenerator), System.Numerics.Tensors, HybridCache, and common .NET parsing libraries.

A note on versions and scope. Library APIs (Document Intelligence, ClosedXML, HtmlAgilityPack, PdfPig, HybridCache, evaluation libraries), service names, and model names change often; compile against the versions you install. The samples show the shape of each technique, are intentionally compact, and omit error handling, retries, and telemetry that production code needs (see AI APIs with .NET and AI Observability). Thresholds and sizes (chunk tokens, score cutoffs, percentiles) are starting points to tune on your own benchmark.

1. Document Ingestion Pipelines

Ingestion is a data-engineering system, not a script

At small scale ingestion is a loop over files. At production scale it is a pipeline that must be incremental, idempotent, observable, resilient to bad inputs, and able to keep the index consistent with the source — including deletions, permission changes, and re-indexing when you change the embedding model or chunking strategy.

SOURCES (file shares, SharePoint, blob storage, wikis, ticketing, databases, web crawls, user uploads)
   │  connectors + change detection (ETag / last-modified / change feed / content hash)
   v
STAGING            raw bytes stored immutably (blob) with source metadata — so you can re-parse without re-fetching
   │
   v
PARSE              format-specific parsers -> a unified document model (headings, paragraphs, tables, lists, pages)
   │  (+ OCR for scanned content)
   v
CLEAN & ENRICH     strip boilerplate, normalize, detect language, extract metadata/tags, attach ACLs, (optionally) summaries/entities
   │
   v
CHUNK              structure-aware / semantic chunks with parent links, neighbor links, section paths
   │
   v
EMBED              batched, cached by content hash, rate-limited, model version recorded
   │
   v
INDEX              vector + keyword + metadata; upsert the new version, then delete superseded chunks
   │
   v
REGISTRY           per-document state: hash, parser version, chunker version, embedding model, status, errors, timestamps

Design rules 

IDEMPOTENT          Re-running on the same input yields the same index state (deterministic chunk IDs built from doc ID + content hash + position).
INCREMENTAL         Process only what changed: compare a content hash (or ETag/modified time) with the registry. Re-embedding unchanged text is pure waste.
STAGED              Persist raw files and intermediate artifacts (parsed document, chunks) so a new chunker or embedding model can be re-run WITHOUT re-downloading or re-OCRing.
VERSIONED           Record parser, chunker, and embedding-model versions per document; a registry query "which documents used embedding model X?" drives migrations.
DELETION-AWARE      Removed or unpublished source documents must disappear from the index (an orphaned chunk keeps answering questions). Detect deletions by diffing the source listing against the registry.
PERMISSION-AWARE    Capture ACLs/tenant at ingestion and re-sync when permissions change — stale ACLs are a data-leak risk (see AI Security, Section 8).
FAULT-ISOLATED      One corrupt PDF must not stop a batch: per-document try/catch, retries for transient errors, a dead-letter queue and a "failed" status with the reason.
BACKPRESSURE        Bounded queues and bounded parallelism so embedding APIs and OCR services aren't flooded (rate limits, cost).
OBSERVABLE          Metrics: documents/hour, failures by stage and type, lag from source change to indexed, tokens embedded, OCR pages, cost; traces per document.
ATOMIC SWAP         Write the new version's chunks, THEN delete the old version's — so documents never briefly vanish from search.
BLUE/GREEN REINDEX  For a new embedding model or schema, build a NEW index alongside the old one, evaluate it, then switch an alias.
SECURE              Parsing is a security boundary: size/page limits, timeouts, sandboxing, malware scanning, and treating extracted text as untrusted (see Section 2).

A unified document model and parser contract 

public enum ElementType { Title, Heading, Paragraph, ListItem, Table, Code, Image, Header, Footer }

public record DocumentElement(
    ElementType Type, string Text, int Level = 0, int? Page = null,
    IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string>? Attributes = null);

public record ParsedDocument(
    string DocId, string Source, string Title, string Language,
    IReadOnlyList<DocumentElement> Elements, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> Metadata);

public record DocumentContext(string DocId, string Source, string FileName, string ContentType, int TenantId, IReadOnlyList<string> AclGroups);

public interface IDocumentParser
{
    bool CanParse(string contentType, string fileName);
    Task<ParsedDocument> ParseAsync(Stream content, DocumentContext context, CancellationToken ct);
}

public record Chunk(
    string Id, string DocId, int Index, string Text, string SectionPath, int? Page,
    string? ParentId = null, string? PrevId = null, string? NextId = null);

public interface IChunker { IReadOnlyList<Chunk> Chunk(ParsedDocument document); }

Everything downstream (chunking, enrichment, indexing) depends only on ParsedDocument. Adding a new file format means adding one parser; improving chunking never touches parsing.

The pipeline orchestrator 

public record IngestionJob(string DocId, string Source, string FileName, string ContentType, int TenantId, IReadOnlyList<string> AclGroups, Func<CancellationToken, Task<Stream>> OpenAsync);

public sealed class IngestionPipeline(
    IEnumerable<IDocumentParser> parsers, IChunker chunker, IEmbeddingGenerator<string, Embedding<float>> embeddings,
    IChunkIndex index, IDocumentRegistry registry, ILogger<IngestionPipeline> log)
{
    private const string EmbeddingModel = "text-embedding-3-small";
    private const string PipelineVersion = "parse-3/chunk-5";                        // bump when parsing or chunking changes -> forces re-processing

    // Consume jobs from a queue with bounded parallelism (backpressure)
    public Task RunAsync(ChannelReader<IngestionJob> jobs, int parallelism, CancellationToken ct) =>
        Parallel.ForEachAsync(jobs.ReadAllAsync(ct), new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = parallelism, CancellationToken = ct },
            async (job, token) =>
            {
                try { await ProcessAsync(job, token); }
                catch (Exception ex)
                {
                    log.LogError(ex, "Ingestion failed for {DocId}", job.DocId);
                    await registry.MarkFailedAsync(job.DocId, ex.GetType().Name, ex.Message, token);     // dead-letter: visible, retryable, never blocks the batch
                }
            });

    private async Task ProcessAsync(IngestionJob job, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await using Stream stream = await job.OpenAsync(ct);
        using var buffer = new MemoryStream();
        await stream.CopyToAsync(buffer, ct);

        string hash = Convert.ToHexString(SHA256.HashData(buffer.ToArray()));
        if (await registry.IsCurrentAsync(job.DocId, hash, PipelineVersion, EmbeddingModel, ct))
            return;                                                                                 // unchanged: skip parse, OCR, embedding

        IDocumentParser parser = parsers.FirstOrDefault(p => p.CanParse(job.ContentType, job.FileName))
            ?? throw new NotSupportedException($"No parser for {job.ContentType}");

        buffer.Position = 0;
        ParsedDocument parsed = await parser.ParseAsync(buffer, new DocumentContext(job.DocId, job.Source, job.FileName, job.ContentType, job.TenantId, job.AclGroups), ct);
        IReadOnlyList<Chunk> chunks = chunker.Chunk(parsed);

        var records = new List<IndexRecord>();
        const int BatchSize = 64;
        for (int i = 0; i < chunks.Count; i += BatchSize)
        {
            var batch = chunks.Skip(i).Take(BatchSize).ToList();
            var vectors = await embeddings.GenerateAsync(batch.Select(c => $"{c.SectionPath}\n\n{c.Text}").ToList(), cancellationToken: ct);   // embed WITH the section path as context

            for (int j = 0; j < batch.Count; j++)
                records.Add(new IndexRecord(batch[j], vectors[j].Vector, job.TenantId, job.AclGroups, hash, EmbeddingModel));
        }

        await index.UpsertAsync(records, ct);                                                        // 1. write the NEW version...
        await index.DeleteSupersededAsync(job.DocId, keepContentHash: hash, ct);                     // 2. ...THEN remove the old one (no gap in search)
        await registry.MarkIndexedAsync(job.DocId, hash, PipelineVersion, EmbeddingModel, chunks.Count, ct);
    }
}

MANAGED ALTERNATIVES  Azure AI Search indexers and integrated vectorization (skillsets that crack documents, chunk, and embed at indexing time), and Azure AI Document Intelligence for parsing, reduce code you must
write and operate — at the cost of less control over chunking and enrichment. A custom pipeline earns its keep when you need structure-aware chunking, custom enrichment, or multi-store indexing.
RUN IT OFF THE REQUEST PATH  BackgroundService/queue workers, Azure Functions, or Container Apps jobs scaled by queue depth (KEDA) — see AI Production / MLOps, Section 7.

Keeping the index in sync with the source 

NEW / CHANGED    Detected by hash/ETag/change feed -> reprocess.
DELETED          Nightly reconciliation: list source IDs, diff against the registry, delete missing documents' chunks.
PERMISSIONS      Subscribe to permission-change events (or re-read ACLs on a schedule) and update the ACL fields on existing chunks WITHOUT re-embedding.
SCHEMA / MODEL   New embedding model or chunker version -> blue/green index build driven by registry queries; keep the old index until the benchmark (Section 19) clears the new one.

2. Parsing PDF, Word, Excel, and HTML

Parsing quality caps retrieval quality

Each format hides structure in a different way, and each loses it differently when flattened to plain text. The goal is not "get the text out" but recover the structure — headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, page numbers — into the unified model so chunking can respect it.

Cross-cutting parsing rules 

DETECT BY CONTENT        Determine the format from the file's bytes (magic numbers), not the extension or the Content-Type header.
LIMITS                   Maximum file size, page/sheet/row counts, decompressed size (zip and "XML bomb" attacks — Office files are ZIP archives), and per-document timeouts.
SANDBOX AND SCAN         Parse in a resource-limited process; scan uploads for malware where policy requires; keep parsing libraries patched (parsers are a classic vulnerability source).
TREAT TEXT AS UNTRUSTED  Documents may contain hidden text (white-on-white, tiny fonts, hidden sheets, comments, display:none HTML) carrying prompt-injection instructions. Strip or flag hidden content and
                         label retrieved text as data at prompt time (see AI Security, Section 2).
PRESERVE STRUCTURE       Headings (with levels), lists, tables as structured text, page numbers, and source locations for citations.
CAPTURE METADATA         Title, author, created/modified dates, language, document type, source URL, version, and ACLs — you cannot filter on metadata you didn't capture.
HANDLE THE ODD CASES     Password-protected files (reject or route to a human), corrupt files (dead-letter), empty extractions (probably scanned — Section 3), and enormous files (split or sample).

PDF 

TEXT-BASED PDFs   A page-description format: glyphs at coordinates, not paragraphs. Libraries such as PdfPig extract words with positions; reading order, multi-column layouts, headers/footers,
                  hyphenation, and tables are the recurring problems.
LAYOUT-AWARE      Azure AI Document Intelligence's layout model returns paragraphs with roles (title, section heading, page header/footer), tables, reading order, and can emit Markdown — usually far better
                  than raw text extraction for complex PDFs.
SCANNED           No text layer at all -> OCR (Section 3).
CLEANUP           Remove repeated page headers/footers and page numbers, rejoin hyphenated words and wrapped lines, normalize whitespace, and keep tables intact.

// PdfPig: words with positions -> paragraphs, with simple header/footer suppression
public sealed class PdfParser : IDocumentParser
{
    public bool CanParse(string contentType, string fileName) => contentType == "application/pdf" || fileName.EndsWith(".pdf", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

    public Task<ParsedDocument> ParseAsync(Stream content, DocumentContext ctx, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        using var pdf = PdfDocument.Open(content);
        var elements = new List<DocumentElement>();

        foreach (var page in pdf.GetPages())
        {
            ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();

            // Reading-order text for the page; production code would also detect columns, tables, and repeated headers/footers
            string text = ContentOrderTextExtractor.GetText(page);
            foreach (string paragraph in text.Split("\n\n", StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries | StringSplitOptions.TrimEntries))
                elements.Add(new DocumentElement(ElementType.Paragraph, Dehyphenate(paragraph), Page: page.Number));
        }

        var meta = new Dictionary<string, string> { ["pages"] = pdf.NumberOfPages.ToString(), ["author"] = pdf.Information.Author ?? "" };
        return Task.FromResult(new ParsedDocument(ctx.DocId, ctx.Source, pdf.Information.Title ?? ctx.FileName, "und", elements, meta));
    }

    private static string Dehyphenate(string s) => Regex.Replace(s.Replace("\r", ""), @"(\w)-\n(\w)", "$1$2").Replace('\n', ' ');
}

// DocumentFormat.OpenXml: walk the body in order, mapping styles to headings and tables to Markdown-style text
public sealed class DocxParser : IDocumentParser
{
    public bool CanParse(string contentType, string fileName) => fileName.EndsWith(".docx", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

    public Task<ParsedDocument> ParseAsync(Stream content, DocumentContext ctx, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        using var doc = WordprocessingDocument.Open(content, isEditable: false);
        Body body = doc.MainDocumentPart!.Document.Body!;
        var elements = new List<DocumentElement>();

        foreach (OpenXmlElement child in body.ChildElements)
        {
            switch (child)
            {
                case Paragraph p when !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(p.InnerText):
                    string? style = p.ParagraphProperties?.ParagraphStyleId?.Val?.Value;           // e.g. "Heading1", "ListParagraph" (verify via the styles part for robustness)
                    if (style is not null && style.StartsWith("Heading", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) && int.TryParse(style[7..], out int level))
                        elements.Add(new DocumentElement(ElementType.Heading, p.InnerText.Trim(), Level: level - 1));
                    else if (style == "Title")
                        elements.Add(new DocumentElement(ElementType.Title, p.InnerText.Trim()));
                    else if (p.ParagraphProperties?.NumberingProperties is not null)
                        elements.Add(new DocumentElement(ElementType.ListItem, "- " + p.InnerText.Trim()));
                    else
                        elements.Add(new DocumentElement(ElementType.Paragraph, p.InnerText.Trim()));
                    break;

                case Table t:
                    elements.Add(new DocumentElement(ElementType.Table, TableToMarkdown(t)));       // keep tables as ONE structured element
                    break;
            }
        }

        string title = doc.PackageProperties.Title ?? ctx.FileName;
        return Task.FromResult(new ParsedDocument(ctx.DocId, ctx.Source, title, "und", elements, new Dictionary<string, string> { ["author"] = doc.PackageProperties.Creator ?? "" }));
    }

    private static string TableToMarkdown(Table table)
    {
        var rows = table.Elements<TableRow>().Select(r => r.Elements<TableCell>().Select(c => c.InnerText.Trim().Replace("|", "/")).ToList()).ToList();
        if (rows.Count == 0) return "";

        var sb = new StringBuilder();
        sb.AppendLine("| " + string.Join(" | ", rows[0]) + " |");
        sb.AppendLine("|" + string.Concat(rows[0].Select(_ => " --- |")));
        foreach (var row in rows.Skip(1)) sb.AppendLine("| " + string.Join(" | ", row) + " |");
        return sb.ToString().TrimEnd();
    }
}

// ClosedXML: each worksheet row becomes a self-describing text record
public IEnumerable<DocumentElement> ParseWorkbook(Stream content)
{
    using var workbook = new XLWorkbook(content);

    foreach (IXLWorksheet sheet in workbook.Worksheets.Where(w => w.Visibility == XLWorksheetVisibility.Visible))
    {
        IXLRange? used = sheet.RangeUsed();
        if (used is null) continue;

        List<string> headers = used.FirstRow().Cells().Select(c => c.GetString().Trim()).ToList();     // assumes row 1 is the header; detect it properly in production

        foreach (IXLRangeRow row in used.RowsUsed().Skip(1))
        {
            var fields = new List<string>();
            for (int i = 0; i < headers.Count; i++)
            {
                string value = row.Cell(i + 1).GetFormattedString();                                    // the displayed value (formulas already evaluated and cached by Excel)
                if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value) && !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(headers[i]))
                    fields.Add($"{headers[i]}: {value}");
            }

            if (fields.Count > 0)
                yield return new DocumentElement(ElementType.Paragraph, $"[Sheet: {sheet.Name}] " + string.Join("; ", fields), Attributes: new Dictionary<string, string> { ["sheet"] = sheet.Name });
        }
    }
}

// HtmlAgilityPack: strip boilerplate and hidden content, keep headings and paragraphs in document order
public sealed class HtmlParser : IDocumentParser
{
    public bool CanParse(string contentType, string fileName) => contentType.StartsWith("text/html");

    public async Task<ParsedDocument> ParseAsync(Stream content, DocumentContext ctx, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var doc = new HtmlDocument();
        doc.Load(content);

        // Remove non-content and (potentially adversarial) hidden elements
        string xpath = "//script|//style|//nav|//footer|//aside|//form|//noscript|//iframe|//comment()" +
                       "|//*[@hidden]|//*[contains(@style,'display:none')]|//*[contains(@style,'visibility:hidden')]";
        foreach (HtmlNode node in doc.DocumentNode.SelectNodes(xpath)?.ToList() ?? [])
            node.Remove();

        HtmlNode main = doc.DocumentNode.SelectSingleNode("//main") ?? doc.DocumentNode.SelectSingleNode("//article") ?? doc.DocumentNode.SelectSingleNode("//body");
        var elements = new List<DocumentElement>();

        foreach (HtmlNode node in main.SelectNodes(".//h1|.//h2|.//h3|.//h4|.//p|.//li|.//pre") ?? Enumerable.Empty<HtmlNode>())
        {
            string text = HtmlEntity.DeEntitize(node.InnerText).Trim();
            if (text.Length == 0) continue;

            elements.Add(node.Name switch
            {
                "h1" or "h2" or "h3" or "h4" => new DocumentElement(ElementType.Heading, text, Level: node.Name[1] - '1'),
                "li" => new DocumentElement(ElementType.ListItem, "- " + text),
                "pre" => new DocumentElement(ElementType.Code, text),
                _ => new DocumentElement(ElementType.Paragraph, text)
            });
        }

        string title = HtmlEntity.DeEntitize(doc.DocumentNode.SelectSingleNode("//title")?.InnerText ?? ctx.FileName);
        string lang = doc.DocumentNode.SelectSingleNode("//html")?.GetAttributeValue("lang", "und") ?? "und";
        return new ParsedDocument(ctx.DocId, ctx.Source, title, lang, elements, new Dictionary<string, string>());
    }
}

3. OCR for Scanned Documents

Scanned pages carry text as pixels

A scanned PDF (or a photo of a document) has no text layer: text extraction returns nothing, and the document silently vanishes from your index. OCR recovers the text — but OCR is the most expensive, slowest, and error-prone stage of ingestion, so it must be applied deliberately.

// Page-level routing: a page with images but almost no extractable text is probably a scan

MITIGATIONS

  LANGUAGE             Detect or specify language per page; wrong language models silently ruin accuracy.

Treat OCR output as untrusted too

OCR'd text can contain instructions (visible or hidden) just like any extracted text, and OCR confidence says nothing about intent. The same prompt-injection and privacy rules apply (see AI Security, Sections 2 and 5): scanned IDs, medical forms, and contracts are sensitive; control where pages are sent and how long extracted text is retained.

4. Semantic Chunking

Splitting where the meaning changes, not where the character count runs out

Fixed-size chunking cuts mid-thought; naive paragraph splitting produces chunks of wildly different sizes. Semantic chunking tries to place boundaries where the topic shifts, so each chunk is about one thing — which makes its embedding sharper and its retrieval more precise.

A hierarchy of strategies — cheapest first 

1. STRUCTURE-AWARE (headings, sections, list and table boundaries)   Free, deterministic, and usually the best default when the parser recovers real structure. Split on headings; keep tables, code
                                                                      blocks, and lists whole; prefix each chunk with its section path.
2. RECURSIVE / BOUNDARY-AWARE   Split on the largest boundary that fits (section -> paragraph -> sentence), packing up to a token budget.
3. EMBEDDING-BASED SEMANTIC     Embed sentences, find where adjacent-sentence similarity drops, and split there (below).
4. LLM-BASED / PROPOSITIONAL    Ask an LLM to split into self-contained propositions or topical segments, rewriting pronouns ("it" -> "the Q3 policy"). High quality; expensive at ingestion; verify no content was lost.
5. LATE CHUNKING               Run a long-context embedding model over the WHOLE document first, then pool token embeddings per chunk, so each chunk's vector reflects document-wide context. Needs a suitable embedding model.
6. CONTEXTUAL ENRICHMENT       Have an LLM write a 1-2 sentence description situating each chunk in its document and prepend it before embedding/indexing — popularized as "contextual retrieval." Complements any chunker.

A structure-aware chunker 

public sealed class StructureAwareChunker(Tokenizer tokenizer, int maxTokens = 400) : IChunker
{
    public IReadOnlyList<Chunk> Chunk(ParsedDocument doc)
    {
        var chunks = new List<Chunk>();
        var headings = new string?[6];                                      // current heading at each level -> the "section path"
        var buffer = new List<string>();
        int bufferTokens = 0;
        int? bufferPage = null;

        void Flush()
        {
            if (buffer.Count == 0) return;
            string path = string.Join(" > ", headings.Where(h => h is not null));
            chunks.Add(new Chunk($"{doc.DocId}:{chunks.Count}", doc.DocId, chunks.Count, string.Join("\n\n", buffer), path, bufferPage));
            buffer.Clear(); bufferTokens = 0; bufferPage = null;
        }

        foreach (DocumentElement el in doc.Elements)
        {
            switch (el.Type)
            {
                case ElementType.Header or ElementType.Footer:
                    continue;                                               // drop page furniture

                case ElementType.Title or ElementType.Heading:
                    Flush();                                                // a new section always starts a new chunk
                    int level = Math.Clamp(el.Level, 0, 5);
                    headings[level] = el.Text;
                    for (int i = level + 1; i < headings.Length; i++) headings[i] = null;
                    break;

                case ElementType.Table:
                    Flush();
                    string tablePath = string.Join(" > ", headings.Where(h => h is not null));
                    chunks.Add(new Chunk($"{doc.DocId}:{chunks.Count}", doc.DocId, chunks.Count, el.Text, tablePath, el.Page));     // a table is never split mid-row (split large tables by row groups with the header repeated)
                    break;

                default:
                    int tokens = tokenizer.CountTokens(el.Text);
                    if (bufferTokens + tokens > maxTokens) Flush();
                    buffer.Add(el.Text);
                    bufferTokens += tokens;
                    bufferPage ??= el.Page;
                    break;
            }
        }
        Flush();

        // Link neighbours so retrieval can expand a hit to the text around it (Section 5)
        for (int i = 0; i < chunks.Count; i++)
            chunks[i] = chunks[i] with { PrevId = i > 0 ? chunks[i - 1].Id : null, NextId = i < chunks.Count - 1 ? chunks[i + 1].Id : null };

        return chunks;
    }
}

An embedding-based semantic chunker 

public sealed class SemanticChunker(
    IEmbeddingGenerator<string, Embedding<float>> embeddings, Tokenizer tokenizer,
    int minTokens = 120, int maxTokens = 500, double breakPercentile = 0.90, int bufferSize = 1)
{
    public async Task<IReadOnlyList<string>> ChunkAsync(string text, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        string[] sentences = Regex.Split(text.Trim(), @"(?<=[.!?])\s+(?=[A-Z0-9""'(])");      // naive splitter; use a proper sentence segmenter for abbreviations, other languages
        if (sentences.Length < 3) return [text];

        // 1. Embed each sentence together with its neighbours — single sentences give noisy similarity signals
        var windows = sentences
            .Select((_, i) => string.Join(" ", sentences.Skip(Math.Max(0, i - bufferSize)).Take(2 * bufferSize + 1)))
            .ToList();
        var vectors = await embeddings.GenerateAsync(windows, cancellationToken: ct);           // batch these calls for large documents

        // 2. Distance between adjacent windows: a spike means the topic changed
        var distances = new double[sentences.Length - 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < distances.Length; i++)
            distances[i] = 1 - TensorPrimitives.CosineSimilarity(vectors[i].Vector.Span, vectors[i + 1].Vector.Span);

        double threshold = Percentile(distances, breakPercentile);                              // split at the top ~10% of distance spikes

        // 3. Build chunks, honoring minimum and maximum sizes so semantics don't produce absurd chunks
        var chunks = new List<string>();
        var current = new List<string>();
        int currentTokens = 0;

        for (int i = 0; i < sentences.Length; i++)
        {
            int tokens = tokenizer.CountTokens(sentences[i]);
            bool topicShift = i > 0 && distances[i - 1] > threshold && currentTokens >= minTokens;
            bool tooBig = current.Count > 0 && currentTokens + tokens > maxTokens;

            if (topicShift || tooBig)
            {
                chunks.Add(string.Join(" ", current));
                current.Clear();
                currentTokens = 0;
            }
            current.Add(sentences[i]);
            currentTokens += tokens;
        }
        if (current.Count > 0) chunks.Add(string.Join(" ", current));
        return chunks;
    }

    private static double Percentile(double[] values, double p)
    {
        double[] sorted = values.OrderBy(v => v).ToArray();
        return sorted[(int)Math.Min(sorted.Length - 1, Math.Floor(p * sorted.Length))];
    }
}

Honest guidance on semantic chunking 

IT'S NOT AUTOMATICALLY BETTER   Studies and practitioner reports show semantic chunking gives modest and inconsistent gains over good structure-aware/recursive chunking on many corpora, at higher ingestion cost
                                (it embeds every sentence window). Start with structure-aware chunking; adopt semantic or LLM-based splitting only if the benchmark (Section 19) shows a retrieval gain on YOUR data.
COST                            Embedding every sentence window multiplies ingestion embedding spend; cache by content hash and run it only for documents without reliable structure (long prose, transcripts).
KEEP SIZE BOUNDS                Always enforce min/max tokens; pure similarity splitting can create tiny fragments or huge chunks.
TABLES / CODE / LISTS           Never split them mid-structure, whatever the similarity says.
TUNE ON RETRIEVAL METRICS       Chunk size, breakpoint percentile, and window size are hyperparameters; sweep them against Recall@k and answer quality, not by eyeballing a few chunks.

5. Chunk Overlap Strategies

Why overlap exists — and what it costs

Without overlap, a fact that straddles a boundary is split across two chunks, and neither chunk alone answers the question. Overlap repeats some boundary text in adjacent chunks as insurance. The price: a larger index, duplicate retrieval hits, and wasted prompt tokens.

The strategies 

NO OVERLAP + NEIGHBOR EXPANSION   Chunks don't overlap; each stores prev/next IDs, and retrieval fetches the neighbors of a hit (Section 6). Cleanest index; usually the better design when you control retrieval.
FIXED TOKEN OVERLAP               Repeat the last N tokens (typically 10-20% of chunk size) at the start of the next chunk. Simple, but can start mid-sentence — look worse and embed oddly.
SENTENCE-LEVEL OVERLAP            Repeat the last 1-2 whole SENTENCES. Boundaries stay clean; the most common practical choice for prose.
PARAGRAPH / SECTION CONTEXT       Instead of repeating body text, repeat the SECTION PATH and (optionally) a short summary of the previous chunk as a prefix. Cheap context without duplicating content.
SLIDING WINDOW                    Overlapping windows over the whole document (high overlap, e.g. 50%); maximizes recall at large index and cost penalty — rarely justified outside small, critical corpora.
STRUCTURE-AWARE (NONE NEEDED)     When chunks are whole sections/tables/list groups, boundaries are natural and overlap adds little.

Sentence-level overlap with guaranteed progress 

public static IEnumerable<string> SlidingSentenceChunks(IReadOnlyList<string> sentences, Tokenizer tokenizer, int maxTokens, int overlapSentences)
{
    int start = 0;

    while (start < sentences.Count)
    {
        int end = start, tokens = 0;

        // Always take at least one sentence, even if it alone exceeds the budget
        while (end < sentences.Count && (end == start || tokens + tokenizer.CountTokens(sentences[end]) <= maxTokens))
        {
            tokens += tokenizer.CountTokens(sentences[end]);
            end++;
        }

        yield return string.Join(" ", sentences.Skip(start).Take(end - start));

        if (end >= sentences.Count) yield break;
        start = Math.Max(start + 1, end - overlapSentences);        // step back by the overlap, but ALWAYS make progress
    }
}

Undoing the cost of overlap at query time

Overlap means two adjacent chunks may both be retrieved, repeating the same sentences in the prompt. Merge adjacent hits from the same document into one passage:

public record Passage(string DocId, string SectionPath, string Text, double Score, IReadOnlyList<string> ChunkIds);

public static IReadOnlyList<Passage> MergeAdjacent(IEnumerable<ScoredChunk> hits)
{
    var passages = new List<Passage>();

    foreach (var docGroup in hits.GroupBy(h => h.Chunk.DocId))
    {
        var ordered = docGroup.OrderBy(h => h.Chunk.Index).ToList();
        var run = new List<ScoredChunk> { ordered[0] };

        for (int i = 1; i < ordered.Count; i++)
        {
            if (ordered[i].Chunk.Index == run[^1].Chunk.Index + 1) run.Add(ordered[i]);        // consecutive chunks: same passage
            else { passages.Add(ToPassage(run)); run = [ordered[i]]; }
        }
        passages.Add(ToPassage(run));
    }
    return passages.OrderByDescending(p => p.Score).ToList();
}

// When concatenating a run, drop the overlapping prefix of each chunk after the first (store the overlap length at ingestion) so repeated sentences aren't injected twice.
static Passage ToPassage(List<ScoredChunk> run) =>
    new(run[0].Chunk.DocId, run[0].Chunk.SectionPath, string.Join("\n", run.Select(r => r.Chunk.Text)), run.Max(r => r.Score), run.Select(r => r.Chunk.Id).ToList());

Rules of thumb 

START WITH LITTLE OR NONE   Prefer clean boundaries + neighbor expansion + a section-path prefix; add 1-2 sentences of overlap only if the benchmark shows boundary-straddling misses.
10-20% IS TYPICAL           If you use token/sentence overlap on prose, 10-20% of the chunk size is the common range. Beyond ~25% you mostly pay for duplicates.
STORE ADJACENCY             chunk_index, prev_id, next_id, and the overlap length — enabling merging and neighbor fetches.
DEDUPLICATE RESULTS         Merge adjacent hits and drop near-duplicates before building the prompt (MMR, Section 12, helps too).
COUNT THE COST              Overlap of 20% adds ~20% to embeddings, index size, and storage — and to the tokens spent whenever neighbors are both retrieved.
MEASURE                     Compare no overlap / sentence overlap / larger chunks on Recall@k and answer quality with the benchmark (Section 19).

6. Parent-Child Retrieval

Precision to find, context to answer

Small chunks embed sharply and match precisely — but a 100-token snippet rarely contains enough context to answer well. Large chunks contain context — but their embeddings blur many topics together, hurting precision. Parent-child (small-to-big) retrieval gets both: index small child chunks, but return their larger parent (the section, or the surrounding text) to the model.

DOCUMENT
  └─ PARENT (a section, ~500-1500 tokens)     <- what the LLM reads         (stored in a document store; NOT necessarily embedded)
        ├─ CHILD 1 (~100-200 tokens)          <- what vector search matches (embedded and indexed, each with parent_id)
        ├─ CHILD 2
        └─ CHILD 3

Variants 

SMALL-TO-BIG (PARENT RETURN)       A child match returns its whole parent section.
SENTENCE-WINDOW RETRIEVAL          Index single sentences; on a hit, return that sentence plus k sentences either side. Maximum precision, flexible context.
AUTO-MERGING                       If several children of the same parent are retrieved (say at least half of them), return the PARENT; otherwise return just the matched children with neighbors. Avoids both fragmentation and bloat.
MULTI-VECTOR RETRIEVAL             Several vectors per parent — the chunks, an LLM-written summary, and hypothetical questions the parent answers — all pointing to the same parent. Queries match whichever phrasing fits.
DOCUMENT-LEVEL PARENTS             Return the whole (short) document when a child matches — right for small documents like FAQs and tickets.
