articles.body_html:
The most connected function in a code graph I opened this week has 124 edges. It doesn't exist.

It is ten Python test helpers called _make_siege, one per test file, plus two TypeScript makeSiege helpers and three lines that define something else entirely, all folded into one node. The graph's report ranks it first among "your core abstractions."

I found that by checking every call edge in the graph against the line it cites. That check only works because a code graph does something grep and embeddings never do.

Three ways to ask what calls what

graphify was on GitHub trending this week, with 1,434 stars in a day and about 131,000 in total. It is a Python CLI plus a /graphify skill for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and about twenty other assistants. It parses code with tree-sitter, with no LLM and no embeddings for the code part, and writes a graph.json of functions, classes and files joined by edges like calls, imports and inherits. You ask it things with graphify query, explain and path. Every edge is tagged EXTRACTED (read straight from the source) or INFERRED (resolved by graphify).

Here is the claim I want to argue. An agent has three ways to find out what a function calls, or what calls it:

  • grep returns lines. Evidence, with no meaning attached. It cannot be wrong about what line 89 says. It can only be noisy.
  • Embeddings return neighbors: chunks that look like your question. No relation, no exact address.
  • A graph returns sentences: mark_changelog_seen calls _require_member_session, at a file and line, with a tag saying how sure it is.

Only the graph makes claims. That is the whole value, because a claim is something an agent can act on without reading twenty files. It is also the risk, because a wrong claim comes out in the same format as a right one, tag and all.

How I checked

I didn't install graphify. It is a Python tool, graphify install registers a skill, and graphify claude install adds a hook to the assistant's settings. I don't run those for a post.

I didn't need to. The repo ships worked examples with their real output, and one of them is a real public codebase: glitchwerks/rsl-siege-manager, a FastAPI backend, a React frontend and a Discord bot in one repo. The case study pins commit 6085fd6 and commits the graph.json graphify built from it in May: 1,886 nodes, 3,876 edges.

So I cloned the app at that commit and wrote a 36-line Node script. Every calls edge carries the file and line of the call, so for each one it reads that line and asks three questions:

for (const e of g.links.filter(l => l.relation === 'calls')) {
  const src = node[e.source], tgt = node[e.target]
  const name = tgt.label.replace(/\(\)$/, '').replace(/^\./, '')
  const text = lineOf(e.source_file, e.source_location)
  const faults = []
  if (family(src.source_file) !== family(tgt.source_file)) faults.push('wrongLanguage')
  if (src.source_file !== e.source_file) faults.push('callerFromOtherFile')
  if (!new RegExp(`(^|[^\\w])${esc(name)}\\s*[(<]`).test(text)) faults.push('nameNotOnLine')
}

Is the caller in the same language as the callee? Is the caller defined in the file where the call happens? Does the cited line actually call something by the callee's name? It ran in under half a second, with identical output both times.

What the check found 

            edges   pass   py<->ts   caller elsewhere   name not on line
EXTRACTED     989    853        83                 57                 84
INFERRED      153    105        34                 33                  7

958 of the 1,142 call edges pass all three checks. 184 fail at least one, and 136 of those are tagged EXTRACTED, the tag that means "read directly from the source."

Most of the failures share one cause: 145 of the 184 touch a node that two or more files claim to contain. Here is one such node with four of its six edges, read from the raw JSON:

markChangelogSeen()                  frontend/src/api/changelog.ts L12
  <-- contains  changelog.ts                EXTRACTED
  <-- contains  changelog.py                EXTRACTED
  --> calls     _require_member_session()   EXTRACTED  backend/app/api/changelog.py:L89
  --> calls     ChangelogStatusResponse     INFERRED   backend/app/api/changelog.py:L95

The real markChangelogSeen is a two-line TypeScript function that sends a POST. The Python endpoint it hits, mark_changelog_seen, has no node of its own. Two of its calls now belong to the TypeScript function, because the graph merged the two by name. The rest of the failures are name matching gone wide: 22 calls to Python's built-in list() point at const list = screen.getByTestId("feature-list") in a TypeScript test.

That happened to a lot of code. Of the 769 top-level Python functions in the graphed files, 200 have no node in their own file, and 164 of those share a name, give or take case and underscores, with a node somewhere else. 121 nodes are claimed by two or more files. Six of the committed report's top ten god nodes are helpers merged across files, led by _make_siege() at 124 edges, _make_member() at 92 and _make_position() at 85.

The case study's review saw that ranking and concluded that test factories pile up edges because every test uses them. A reasonable reading of the report. One command says otherwise:

$ grep -rln "def _make_siege(" . | wc -l
      10

That is the difference between evidence and a claim. grep showed ten functions. The graph had already decided there was one.

In fairness, this was fixed

The merges came from the dedup pass, which matched labels by fuzzy similarity, a sensible thing for doc concepts and a wrong one for code. Issue #1205, opened June 9, reported a single --update dropping about 1,300 nodes from a 6,000-node graph. It was fixed the next day: code nodes are now keyed by ID only and never label-merged. Version 0.9.0 put the full path into every node ID. Cross-language INFERRED calls are dropped at build time. The current release is 0.9.93.

I read those fixes in the source. I did not run the current version, so I can't say what it builds from this repo today. The committed graph has not been rebuilt since May, and the docs still point at the worked folders as output you can check.

What interests me is the changelog itself. It reads like a field guide to wrong edges: short names like log and find collecting hundreds of spurious calls (#543), an npm import landing on an unrelated Python file as an EXTRACTED edge (#1638), three phantom edges that were the only bridge between 2,409 Python nodes and 1,403 TypeScript nodes (#1749). Each got fixed. The class of bug stays, because resolving a call means deciding which of several same-named things it meant, and that is always a judgment.

How I'd use one

Treat every edge as a citation, not a fact. The current graphify explain prints the call site next to each edge, so checking one is a single read. Do that read before acting on any edge that would change code.

For "who calls this" before a rename or a delete, use the graph for the shortlist and grep for the completeness. A graph that misses a caller gives no sign of it. grep's noise is visible: you read it.

Watch the install's defaults, too. The always-on hook tells the agent it "MUST run graphify query" before grepping. The same message says to read raw files once the graph has named the lines. Keep that second half, because that read is what makes the first half safe.

The limits of my check: it only catches faults that show on the cited line, so a call bound to the wrong same-language twin passes, and 184 is a floor. And it is one repo, graphed five months ago. The project's own code benchmark, 82.0% key-fact coverage against 70.8% for a grep-and-read baseline, rests on six questions.

When your agent's tool says "A calls B," what does it check before it believes it?

articles.title: Matita 0.4.0: 60 new icons, and one number from sketchy to exact
articles.description: Matita is a set of pencil-style icons for the web, drawn by code. Lines run a little past their ends,...
articles.body_html:
Matita is a set of pencil-style icons for the web, drawn by code. Lines run a little past their ends, box corners cross, circles overlap where the pen closes. 0.4.0 is out today: 60 new icons (200 to 260) and a new setting called wobble that goes from the full sketchy hand all the way down to exact shapes.

If you haven't seen it, the first post explains the engine: [LINK to the first dev.to article]. The short version is that every icon is a line of plotted shapes, and a small deterministic engine adds the pencil habits, so the same name always draws the same way. This post is about what changed.

60 new icons, mostly what people asked for

When I posted the set, the most concrete request in the comments was a medical and science set. So that is the biggest group: 22 icons.

stethoscope, syringe, pill, test-tube, microscope, thermometer, heart-pulse, medical-cross, bandage, radiation, x-ray, dna, atom, brain, tooth, bone, ambulance, hospital-bed, mars, venus, face-mask, pipette.

The other 38 fill everyday gaps: people and files (user-check, file-check, folder-plus, mail-open), tools, devices and places (wrench, hammer, plug, keyboard, cpu, store, car, plane), and things you reach for all the time (timer, calculator, receipt, qr-code, trophy, percent, shuffle, repeat).

Every glyph still goes through the same checks: a contact sheet at 96 px and at 24 px, a bounds check with the stroke included, and a lint. That caught real things. A fingerprint read as wifi at 24 px, so it is not in the set. Six of the new icons (brain, x-ray, microscope, pipette, wrench, car) were drawn twice because the first version did not read: the first brain looked like a butterfly, so it is now a top view with two hemispheres; the first car could have been a bus, so it has a sloped roof and bigger windows now.

Not in this release: Greek letters, a lab coat and a surgeon. I couldn't draw them clearly at 24 px yet. If you need them, say which ones.

Wobble: one number, from sketchy to exact

The part I wanted most is the setting. The sketchy default is the point of the set, but there are places where you want the same icon calmer, or exactly straight.

import { SketchIcon } from '@matita/icons/react';

<SketchIcon name="wrench" />              // the full hand (default, wobble 1)
<SketchIcon name="wrench" wobble={0.4} /> // a calm hand
<SketchIcon name="wrench" wobble={0} />   // exact shapes

)

Plain JavaScript works too, and so do your own glyphs:

import { drawIcon } from '@matita/icons/engine';
import { toSvg } from '@matita/icons';

toSvg(drawIcon('calendar', { wobble: 0 }), { size: 24 });

How it works

Every habit of the pencil in the engine already had an amount: how far a line overshoots its end, how much it bows, how much a point jitters, how far a ring overlaps. Wobble multiplies those amounts:

const K = wobble, S = v => K === 1 ? v : v * K;
const j = a => (r() * 2 - 1) * a * K;          // jitter
const e1 = S(ov) * (.45 + r() * .9);           // overshoot

Two things follow from that. First, at wobble = 1 every expression multiplies by nothing, so the default draws exactly what 0.3.0 drew. I checked it with a hash over 200 glyphs at 6 seeds before and after the change: identical. Second, the random numbers come from the same stream whatever the wobble is, so 0.5 is the same drawing as 1, just calmer, not a different one. Sliding the number looks like one icon relaxing instead of flickering between takes.

At wobble = 0 the engine takes a different path: it stops sketching and draws the shapes as they are plotted. True lines, circles and ellipses as two arcs, arcs, curves, and closed shapes with square corners. There is no jitter left, so an exact icon does not depend on the seed.

Exact icons are also small. An average exact SVG is about 0.47 KB raw (0.26 KB gzipped), against about 0.82 KB (0.45 KB) for the sketchy one. There are ready-made files for all 260 at @matita/icons/exact/<name>.svg, so you can use them without running any code. The pencil variant also works over exact shapes.

Try the slider on matita.dev: there is a Wobble slider and a Perfect button next to the seed, and the copy snippets follow.

Also new on the site

  • matita.dev/changelog/ says when each icon arrived, and the icon browser shows an "Added in" label with a New badge on the latest ones.
  • matita.dev/roadmap/ is the public list of what is shipped, what is being built and what is next. Targets move.
  • matita.dev/llms.txt and matita.dev/icons.json list every icon with the version it arrived in, so an assistant (or a script) can check that a name exists instead of guessing.

Using it 

npm i @matita/icons

React components, plain SVG files, a script tag, a sprite and the Figma file are all there. It is MIT, free for personal and commercial projects, no signup. The Figma file is at https://www.figma.com/community/file/1688850201209755442 <!-- publish the Figma update to 260 icons before posting -->.

What's next

On the roadmap: search by meaning (type "delete", find the bin) targeted for November, and more science glyphs for December depending on requests. If an icon you need is missing, open an icon request. New glyphs are a line of shapes each, so they're quick to add, and 0.4.0 is mostly proof of that: 60 of them came from one list.

articles.title: Give Your AI Feature a Kill Switch, a Budget, and a Paper Trail
articles.description: The second-most dangerous demo is "watch the agent do everything." The most dangerous is shipping...
articles.body_html:
The second-most dangerous demo is "watch the agent do everything." The most dangerous is shipping that demo to real users on Monday.

I build web and mobile products with Node, React, and Flutter, and I speak about AI in community spaces. The pattern I keep seeing: teams add a chat box or an "AI assistant" tab, wire an API key, and hope prompt vibes will behave in production. Hope is not an architecture.

This post is a practical starter kit for fullstack builders: three controls every AI feature should have before you invite non-technical users — a kill switch, a budget, and a paper trail. No cloud-vendor lock-in assumed. You can implement these with boring Node middleware and a small React admin panel.

Why demos lie

Figure: gate every model call — kill switch, budget, paper trail.

In a Meetup demo:

  • You are the only user
  • You type polite, on-distribution prompts
  • You ignore the bill
  • You can Ctrl+C when it loops
  • Nobody pastes a 40-page PDF of junk to "summarize"

In production:

  • Users paste secrets by accident
  • Prompts go adversarial or just confused
  • A retry storm turns into a surprise invoice
  • An agent tool call hits the wrong environment
  • You need to explain what happened three days later

Governance sounds enterprise. The core is simpler: assume the model will be wrong, expensive, or both — and design the blast radius.

Control 1: Kill switch (feature flags that actually stop spend)

A kill switch is not a blog toggle in Notion. It is a runtime gate checked before every model call and every tool invocation.

Minimal shape:

// lib/aiFlags.js
export async function assertAiEnabled(featureKey) {
  const row = await db.flags.get(featureKey);
  if (!row?.enabled) {
    const err = new Error("AI_FEATURE_DISABLED");
    err.code = "AI_FEATURE_DISABLED";
    throw err;
  }
}

Call it at the edge of your AI service:

export async function runAssistant({ userId, featureKey, input }) {
  await assertAiEnabled(featureKey);
  // ... budget check, then model call
}

Wire a React admin (or even a secured POST /admin/flags) so you can disable meetup-copilot without redeploying. When something smells wrong at 1 a.m., you want a button — not a pipeline.

Mobile note: Flutter clients should treat AI_FEATURE_DISABLED as a first-class UI state ("Assistant temporarily off"), not a generic 500. Users forgive maintenance; they do not forgive spinning forever.

Bonus: scoped kills

Prefer per-feature flags over a global "AI off":

  • chat.summarize
  • chat.reply-suggest
  • agent.tools.github (keep this off until you are truly ready)

That way a broken experimental agent does not take down a simple title-rewriter that still helps organizers.

Control 2: Budget (tokens, calls, and blast radius)

If you cannot answer "what is the max this feature can cost today?", you do not have a product — you have an open tab.

Soft limits per user / per org 

export async function assertWithinBudget({ tenantId, featureKey }) {
  const usage = await db.usage.today(tenantId, featureKey);
  const limit = await db.limits.get(tenantId, featureKey);

  if (usage.calls >= limit.maxCalls || usage.tokens >= limit.maxTokens) {
    const err = new Error("AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED");
    err.code = "AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED";
    throw err;
  }
}

Practical defaults for an early community product:

  • Cap calls per user per day
  • Cap max input characters (reject the 2MB paste early)
  • Cap max tool iterations for agents (e.g. 5 steps, then stop with a clear message)
  • Separate "playground" keys from "production" keys

Hard limits at the provider

Also set provider-side spending caps where they exist. Application budgets fail closed when Redis hiccups; provider caps fail closed when your app has a bug. Use both.

Agents need step budgets, not vibes

If you are building anything agent-like (tool calling, multi-step plans):

  • Maximum steps
  • Maximum wall-clock time
  • Allowlist of tools (read calendar ✗ delete calendar until proven)
  • Human confirmation for irreversible actions

Pausing / resuming agents is a hot topic for a reason: long-running autonomy without checkpoints is how you get surprise side effects. Even a simple job table with status: running | paused | done | failed beats an unbounded while-loop in memory.

Control 3: Paper trail (logs you can defend)

When someone asks "why did the assistant tell my users X?", screenshots are not enough.

Log structured events:

await db.aiEvents.insert({
  id: crypto.randomUUID(),
  tenantId,
  userId,
  featureKey,
  model,
  promptVersion,      // e.g. "rsvp-helper@3"
  inputHash,          // hash raw input; store raw only if policy allows
  toolCalls: [...],   // names + args summaries
  outputHash,
  tokensIn,
  tokensOut,
  latencyMs,
  createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
});

Privacy-aware defaults

  • Prefer hashes + short redacted previews over full prompts for sensitive products
  • Never log API keys, auth headers, or payment fields
  • Define retention (30/90 days) and stick to it
  • Make "export my AI history / delete my AI history" a real endpoint if you serve EU users or simply respect people

Prompt versioning is underrated

Store prompts in git (prompts/rsvp-helper.v3.md) and send promptVersion with every call. When behavior changes, you can diff. "The model got dumber" is often "we edited the prompt on Tuesday and forgot."

A thin React admin that earns its keep

You do not need a full observability suite on day one. A single authenticated page with:

  • Feature flags table + toggle
  • Today's spend / call counts per feature
  • Last 50 AI events (status, latency, error code)
  • Big red "disable all AI features" button

…will save you more pain than another model provider abstraction.

How this maps to a real feature

Suppose you add "Suggest event description" for organizers:

  1. Flag: events.ai.suggest-description (default off in prod until soak test)
  2. Budget: 20 suggestions / organizer / day, 1k max input chars
  3. Paper trail: prompt version + hashes + tokens
  4. UX: show the suggestion as a diff the human must accept — never auto-publish
  5. Kill: if suggestions degrade, flip the flag; the rest of the app keeps working

That is product engineering. The model is a dependency, not the product.

Takeaways

  1. Kill switches belong in the request path, not in a document.
  2. Budgets need daily caps, input caps, and agent step caps — plus provider hard limits.
  3. Paper trails need structured events, prompt versions, and privacy rules.
  4. Human confirmation for irreversible actions is not optional.
  5. Ship AI as a flaggable slice of a working app, not as the app's only spine.

If you are adding your first assistant to a Node/React or Flutter app, start with these three controls before you polish the avatar animation. Cool UI with no blast-radius design is how demos become incidents.

What control do you wish you had added earlier — flag, budget, or audit log? I am curious what broke first for other builders.

articles.title: 90% of the AI Agents Clients Ask For Are Just a Cron Job and One API Call
articles.description: A founder asked me to build an autonomous AI agent that monitors their reviews around the clock.  I...
articles.body_html:
A founder asked me to build an autonomous AI agent that monitors their reviews around the clock.

I nodded, asked what the agent should actually do, and listened.

Every hour, someone needs to read the new Google reviews. The negative ones must reach the founder fast. That is the whole job.

Here is what I shipped.

A cron job. One LLM call per review. A Slack webhook.

That is it. No agent framework. No elaborate reasoning loop. No vector database. No memory store.

Every hour, the job pulls reviews posted since the last run. Each review goes to the model exactly once with one instruction: summarize this and flag it if it is negative. The negative ones land in the founder's Slack channel. Everything else gets logged and ignored.

It runs perfectly, costs almost nothing, and the founder loves it.

The whole system

One cron line:

0 * * * * /usr/bin/node /home/app/review-watch.js

One small script:

// review-watch.js: read new reviews, flag the bad ones, ping Slack
import OpenAI from "openai";

const openai = new OpenAI({ apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY });

async function main() {
  const since = new Date(Date.now() - 60 * 60 * 1000).toISOString();
  const reviews = await fetchNewReviews(since); // your reviews API here

  for (const review of reviews) {
    const verdict = await openai.chat.completions.create({
      model: "gpt-4o-mini",
      messages: [
        {
          role: "system",
          content: "Classify this review as positive, neutral or negative. Reply with one word, then a one line summary.",
        },
        { role: "user", content: review.text },
      ],
    });

    const [label, summary] = verdict.choices[0].message.content.split("\n");

    if (label.trim().toLowerCase() === "negative") {
      await postToSlack(`Negative review from ${review.author}: ${summary}`);
    }
  }
}

async function postToSlack(text) {
  await fetch(process.env.SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ text }),
  });
}

main().catch((err) => {
  console.error(err);
  process.exit(1);
});

Two moving parts. You can read the entire system in one sitting.

Why this beat the agent

An agent would have added a planning loop, tool definitions, retry orchestration and state management. For what? The input is fixed: new reviews. The schedule is fixed: every hour. The output is fixed: a Slack message for the bad ones. There is no branching decision to make, no tool to choose, no memory to carry between runs.

Every layer an agent adds on top of that is a layer you get to debug at 3am. A script fails in obvious ways: the cron log tells you exactly which line broke. An agent fails in interesting ways: a tool call went sideways three steps deep inside a reasoning chain and nobody can reproduce it.

Selling an agent when a script would do is how projects get slow and expensive.

The honest framework

Build the agent when the job has real decision making:

  • The system must choose between tools based on what it reads
  • The path branches on intermediate results, not on fixed rules
  • It needs memory across steps to finish a single task
  • The input is ambiguous enough that one fixed prompt cannot handle it

Ship the script when the job looks like this:

  • It runs on a schedule or on a trigger
  • The inputs are known and the outputs are known
  • The model does one well defined thing, like classify or summarize
  • You can read the whole system in one file

Most of the agent requests I get land in the second list. That is not a failure of ambition. It is good engineering: the simplest system that does the job.

One note on cost

This runs one small model call per review, once an hour. There is no framework overhead, no repeated reasoning passes, no state store to maintain. The bill is a rounding error and the founder has never once asked what it costs. Compare that to an agent looping through a large model for the same hourly job and the difference pays for itself.

What is the most overbuilt "AI agent" you have seen? Or built? Drop it in the comments.

I'm Sohail Khan, a Senior Full Stack Developer building AI agents and automation. Tech Lead at LoopxCorp. I write about backend engineering, AI integration and practical system design.

articles.title: ffmpeg.wasm to WebCodecs: the 12x Gap, What Broke, and What Still Can't Move
articles.description: When we built the local-processing mode of our media toolbox (meicut.com) — 20+ tools that trim,...
articles.body_html:
When we built the local-processing mode of our media toolbox (meicut.com) — 20+ tools that trim, compress, convert, and filter video and audio entirely in the browser — the first version bet everything on ffmpeg.wasm. It felt like the obvious choice. Within weeks, the hot paths moved to WebCodecs hardware encoding, ffmpeg.wasm survives as a fallback plus the tools that sit at hard boundaries — audio processing, speed change, AVI/GIF output, reverse — and we have a precise map of where each technology's real boundaries are.

This is the full story: why we started with WASM, the three technology-inherent problems that forced the migration, how the WebCodecs pipeline works, and the decision framework we now use to route each tool.

Why we chose ffmpeg.wasm first (and it was the right call)

Our backend already processed everything server-side with the ffmpeg CLI. That made ffmpeg.wasm almost unfairly attractive:

1. Zero redesign of processing semantics. Our server code was full of carefully-tuned filter graphs — -ss/-t input-side seeking for cuts, even-dimension rounding for crops, maskedmerge + geq three-plane masks for mosaic regions. With ffmpeg.wasm, the browser executor could reuse these line by line. Local and cloud outputs were identical by construction.

2. Complete capability coverage. ffmpeg handles every container, codec, and filter we needed: atempo for audio speed, MP3/FLAC encoding, AVI/GIF muxing, complex filter chains. WebCodecs, by contrast, is a codec primitive — it encodes and decodes raw frames. It doesn't demux your MKV, it doesn't resample your audio, and it definitely doesn't do WSOLA time-stretching.

3. 28 tools, one UI. Because the processing semantics came for free, we could share the entire frontend between cloud and local modes and ship every tool at once.

We knew WebCodecs existed. We also knew its caveats: uneven browser support, no MP3/FLAC encoders, and opaque hardware encoder behavior. Betting on WASM first let us ship. That sequencing mattered — if we'd started with WebCodecs, we'd have spent weeks just on demuxing before shipping a single tool.

Problem 1: Slow, and it sounded like a jet engine

ffmpeg.wasm's x264 is software encoding compiled to WASM — no SIMD in practice, no hardware acceleration. Compressing a high-resolution 2.5K clip made laptop fans spin up like we were mining crypto. Competitors using WebCodecs hardware encoding were silent and an order of magnitude faster. Our benchmark: same 10.5 MB / 720p / 10 s file, medium quality, median of 3 runs on the same machine:

Path Time (median of 3) Output
ffmpeg.wasm (soft x264, incl. 32 MB engine download) 26.5 s 1.27 MB
WebCodecs (hardware H.264) 2.3 s 5.78 MB

(The output sizes differ because the two paths use different rate-control strategies — more on that below. Both were visually fine; the point is the 12× speed gap and the fan noise.)

For a free tool whose entire pitch is "it just works in your browser", CPU-bound software encoding is a UX ceiling you can't design around.

Problem 2: Outputs that came out bigger

Pure CRF rate control targets quality, not size. Feed it an already-lean source (3.30 Mbps) and CRF 28 happily produces a larger file (3.91 Mbps). Users compress a video to make it smaller; an output that grows is a bug report waiting to happen, no matter how defensible the encoding theory is.

CRF-driven inflation is the flavor we first hit, and it is squarely a WASM-path failure. But "outputs that come out bigger" is not exclusive to WASM: the hardware encoder in WebCodecs uses target-bitrate semantics and will happily spend the whole budget — without a per-pixel ceiling, a low-res "smaller" encode can land at 5 Mbps just because the target said so. The dual ceiling in the migration section is what stops that on both paths.

Problem 3: The 32 MB engine bootstrap is a reliability surface

The WASM engine is a ~32 MB download (core JS + WASM + worker), fetched on first use. Around that download sits an entire bootstrap chain — progress reporting, caching, ff.load() initialization, pthread startup for the multi-threaded core — and we learned that every link in that chain can fail silently:

  • Our progress denominator was an estimate (34,135,000 bytes); the real download was 32,849,385 bytes — 96.2% of it. So the bar froze at "96%" even on healthy loads, and users reasonably read that as a hang. (Fix: exact byte counts per engine file, updated every time the core package is bumped.)

  • On some machines, ff.load() never resolved — no error, no rejection, just silence. We added a 60 s watchdog that terminates the attempt and falls back to the single-threaded core.

  • We ultimately traced one production-wide outage of this bootstrap to a server configuration bug of our own making — a missing HTTP response header that Chrome requires before it will construct a module worker. But the larger lesson stood: the engine bootstrap is infrastructure, with the failure modes of infrastructure — while WebCodecs has no bootstrap at all. The browser already contains everything it needs.

That contrast is what turned "WASM is slow" into "the hot paths should not depend on a downloadable engine at all".

The WebCodecs migration

The pipeline 

input file
  → mediabunny (demux; we use it for muxing too — MP4 with faststart)
  → VideoDecoder (hardware) → optional per-frame canvas processing
  → VideoEncoder (hardware H.264)
  → audio: copied passthrough when container-compatible, transcoded otherwise

First interaction runs immediately — no warmup, no download progress, no load watchdog.

hwOrSw: hardware first, always a way back

Every migrated tool is wrapped in the same pattern:

async function hwOrSw<T>(hw: () => Promise<T>, sw: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  try {
    return await hw()
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof LocalCancelledError) throw e // user cancel: never "fall back" into more work
    console.warn('[local] hardware path failed, falling back to wasm:', e)
    return sw()
  }
}

Any failure in the hardware path — unsupported codec, decode error, encode error — silently lands on the proven WASM executor. A localStorage flag forces all-software for production debugging.

The stall watchdog

Individual files can freeze hardware decoders/encoders silently. We carried over the lesson from the engine-load watchdog: bounded waits, never infinite hangs. If progress doesn't advance for 30 seconds, we abandon the hardware attempt and fall back.

Rate control: the dual ceiling that stopped inflation

Hardware encoders use target bitrate semantics — they spend the whole budget, unlike CRF which backs off on easy content. And we needed a guarantee: output must be smaller than input. Two caps, take the minimum:

target = min(
  sourceVideoBitrate × qualityRatio,      // 0.8 / 0.6 / 0.4 — guarantees smaller
  outputPixels × fps × bpp                 // quality ceiling: 0.2 / 0.15 / 0.1
)

The first term kills the reverse-inflation bug. The second is the subtle one: without a bits-per-pixel ceiling, a 480p "smaller" compression would cheerfully burn 5 Mbps of hardware-encoder budget because the target said so.

Preflight with real dimensions

H.264 level support varies with resolution/bitrate/framerate. Asking VideoEncoder.isConfigSupported() about a hypothetical config misses machines that encode 480p fine but choke on 4K. We probe with the actual output dimensions before committing to the hardware path.

The honest hard-boundary list: what stays on WASM

A full audit of every tool produced the list WebCodecs advocates rarely publish — what it genuinely cannot do today:

Tool / capability Why WebCodecs can't Stays on
Audio speed change atempo is WSOLA time-stretching; WebCodecs has no audio processing at all WASM
MP3 / FLAC export Browser AudioEncoder has no MP3 or FLAC encoders; output contracts would break WASM
Volume adjust, audio convert, audio cut Same MP3/FLAC encoder gap WASM
Reverse video Needs every frame in memory to play backwards; large inputs OOM the tab WASM
AVI / GIF output mediabunny has no muxer for either container WASM
Most video filters ffmpeg eq uses offset semantics; CSS/canvas uses multiply — visually different results. Only three presets (grayscale/sepia/invert) are pixel-equivalent WASM for the rest
Crop with pan / custom background Our canvas center-crop covers the common cases; edge semantics differ WASM
Multi-segment cuts with fades Crossfade filter graphs have no streaming equivalent WASM

Everything else — compress, mute, rotate, flip, format conversion (MP4/MOV/MKV/WebM), single-segment trim, center crop, mosaic blur, sketch effect — runs on hardware.

The decision framework we ended up with 

Is the capability expressible as decode → optional canvas → encode?
├─ No (audio processing, exotic containers, complex filter graphs)
│    → ffmpeg.wasm, and that's final
└─ Yes
     → Does the browser support it with THESE dimensions/codec?
          ├─ Yes → WebCodecs hardware path
          │         (30 s stall watchdog, any error → wasm)
          └─ No  → ffmpeg.wasm

Three principles held up across the whole migration:

  1. Bounded waits everywhere. Both paths have watchdogs (60 s engine load, 30 s stall). Silent infinite hangs are the defining failure mode of in-browser media processing; every wait must have a ceiling and a fallback.

  2. Fallbacks are architecture, not error handling. hwOrSw isn't a try/catch — it's the product. Users on odd hardware get slower results, never failed ones.

  3. Match the technology to the capability, not the other way round. WASM-first got us coverage and correctness; WebCodecs-second got us speed where it matters. Neither was a mistake — the mistake would have been treating either one as the whole answer.

The result: the tools people actually hammer (compress, convert, trim) run at hardware speed with no engine download, the long tail still works everywhere ffmpeg works, and the 32 MB WASM engine only ships to browsers that genuinely need it.

This pipeline powers the local-processing mode at meicut.com, where you can try both paths on your own files.

articles.title: Building a Chrome Extension That Compares UI Elements Across Pages
articles.description: Chrome DevTools offers powerful capabilities for inspecting web interfaces.  But when reviewing...
articles.body_html:
Chrome DevTools offers powerful capabilities for inspecting web interfaces.

But when reviewing visual consistency across a product, I often find that the challenge isn't inspecting one element. It's comparing several elements across different screens.

Consider a checkout flow with buttons appearing on different pages. You might want to check whether their typography, padding, colors, and borders are consistent.

Individually inspecting each button and manually comparing its CSS properties becomes repetitive.

I wanted a lightweight tool that could capture those properties, preserve them across navigation, and display the differences in one place.

That idea became Visqora, a free Chrome extension built with React, TypeScript, WXT, and Manifest V3.

What started as a small inspection tool turned into an interesting exercise in browser architecture, asynchronous communication, state management, privacy, and production reliability.

01. Defining the problem

The original goal was straightforward:

Make it easier to compare the computed visual properties of DOM elements, even when those elements belong to different pages.

There was also an important boundary to establish.

Visqora isn't a screenshot regression testing tool.

It doesn't compare images, evaluate visual baselines, or automatically determine whether differences represent defects.

Instead, it compares selected computed CSS properties from DOM elements.

The distinction matters because a different value isn't necessarily an error. Two components may intentionally use different spacing or colors.

Visqora exposes the differences and leaves their interpretation to the developer, QA professional, or designer.

For the initial release, I limited the comparison workspace to five elements.

That constraint kept both the interface and the underlying data model manageable.

02. Architecture across execution contexts

A Chrome extension is not a conventional single-context React application.

Manifest V3 separates functionality across execution environments with different lifecycles and permissions.

Visqora uses three principal contexts:

React Side Panel: The interface where users start inspection, view captured properties, and compare elements.

Background service worker: The orchestration layer responsible for runtime messages, active-tab state, inspection sessions, workspace mutations, and persistence.

Injected inspector: An isolated-world script responsible for interacting with the inspected webpage and capturing computed styles.

These contexts communicate through explicit messages and shared TypeScript contracts.

Architecture overview 

flowchart TB
    U["User"]

    subgraph UI["React Side Panel"]
        P["InspectorPanel"]
        C["Pure comparison engine"]
    end

    subgraph BG["MV3 Background Service Worker"]
        W["Message orchestration"]
        L["Inspection lifecycle"]
        WS["Workspace management"]
    end

    subgraph PAGE["Inspected webpage"]
        I["On-demand injected inspector"]
        D["Page DOM and computed styles"]
    end

    S[("chrome.storage.session")]

    U --> P
    P <-->|"Runtime messages"| W
    W --> L
    W --> WS
    W <-->|"Commands and captures"| I
    I <-->|"DOM inspection"| D
    WS <-->|"Persist and restore"| S
    P --> C
    C --> P

Figure 1. Visqora's execution contexts and their main responsibilities.

The diagram illustrates a deliberate separation of concerns.

The Side Panel does not directly inspect the webpage or mutate the authoritative workspace.

The injected inspector doesn't manage the React interface or long-lived comparison data.

The background service worker coordinates the operation and owns workspace mutations.

That separation introduces messaging overhead, but it also gives each component a clearer responsibility.

03. On-demand injection and minimal access

One decision I wanted to preserve was avoiding unnecessary access to webpages.

Visqora doesn't inject a persistent inspector into every page the user visits.

Instead, inspection starts through an explicit user action.

When the user clicks Inspect, the Side Panel requests permission for the current HTTP or HTTPS origin.

The background worker then attempts to communicate with an existing inspector.

If no inspector is available, it uses chrome.scripting.executeScript() to inject the inspector and retries the activation command.

The inspector runs in Chrome's isolated world.

It creates the hover overlay and registers the event listeners needed to identify and capture elements.

When inspection stops, it cleans up the overlay and listeners.

This approach reduces unnecessary interaction with webpages, but it also creates additional lifecycle and orchestration complexity.

The background worker must account for injection failures, navigation, stale requests, and repeated activation.

There is a clear trade-off:

Less persistent page access means more responsibility for correct activation and cleanup.

04. Capturing snapshots instead of DOM elements

Once inspection is active, Visqora uses pointer events to identify the element under the cursor.

The overlay highlights the current target.

When the user selects an element, the inspector creates a serializable snapshot.

The implementation uses getComputedStyle() to read a specific allowlist of 18 CSS properties.

It also captures a generated identifier, the element's tag name, and a bounded structural selector.

A simplified conceptual flow:

DOM element
    ↓
getComputedStyle()
    ↓
Extract 18 supported properties
    ↓
Normalize values
    ↓
Create serializable capture
    ↓
Send capture to background worker
    ↓
Add trusted source metadata
    ↓
Store snapshot in comparison workspace

The important decision is that Visqora stores a snapshot, not a live DOM reference.

A DOM element belongs to a particular document and can disappear after navigation.

A serializable snapshot can remain useful after that document no longer exists.

The background worker adds source metadata such as the originating tab, URL, document identity when available, and capture timestamp.

This also establishes a privacy boundary.

The snapshot extractor does not copy arbitrary HTML, text content, form values, or DOM references into the comparison workspace.

The limitation is equally important: snapshots represent point-in-time values. They don't automatically update when the original element changes.


Figure 2. Single-element inspection showing grouped CSS properties.

05. A pure comparison engine

The comparison engine is deliberately independent of browser APIs.

It receives captured snapshots and produces an ordered set of property comparisons.

For each supported property, it compares the stored values and marks the property as different when values do not match.

Whitespace is normalized, but the engine doesn't attempt deeper semantic equivalence.

For example, it doesn't claim that all differently formatted CSS color values or length units are necessarily equivalent.

This is intentional.

The comparison engine identifies differences in the recorded data. It doesn't attempt to become a full CSS interpretation engine.

The Side Panel chooses its presentation based on the number of snapshots:

  • With one snapshot, it displays a grouped property inspector.
  • With two to five snapshots, it displays a comparison table.

Because the engine is pure, the comparison rules can be tested independently of Chrome APIs, DOM access, and React rendering.

That separation made the feature easier to maintain and reason about.


Figure 3. Comparison between two or more elements, highlighting property differences.

06. State management across pages and tabs

Cross-page comparison introduces a lifecycle problem.

The webpage being inspected can navigate, reload, or disappear.

The Side Panel can also close.

And under Manifest V3, the background service worker should not be treated as a permanently running process.

The solution was to distinguish two kinds of state.

Active inspection state

Inspection is tied to the current browser context.

The worker tracks tab, session, operation, and document identity where available.

When navigation or a tab switch invalidates the current inspection, the active interaction is stopped or reset.

Visqora doesn't silently reactivate inspection on the new page.

The user must explicitly start it again.

Comparison workspace

Captured snapshots are different.

They remain useful even when inspection ends.

Visqora preserves them through chrome.storage.session, which allows the workspace to survive navigation and Side Panel reopening within the supported browser session.

The background worker is the single owner of workspace mutations.

To prevent concurrent storage operations from overwriting one another, mutations are serialized through a promise queue.

Stored snapshots are also validated when restored rather than blindly trusted.

This architecture preserves the user's comparison work without treating the current webpage as permanent.

07. Handling stale messages

One subtle challenge in browser extensions is asynchronous timing.

Imagine a user starting inspection and then navigating before the operation finishes.

An injection result, element capture, or state update may arrive after the original document has been replaced.

Without additional checks, the application could associate stale data with the current session.

Visqora addresses this by validating the identities associated with operations and captures.

The background worker checks relevant tab, session, operation, and document information before accepting events.

Document IDs aren't guaranteed to be available for every operation, so the system uses the identities that are available.

This is an important distinction between simply sending messages and designing a reliable message protocol.

A response is not necessarily valid just because it arrived successfully. It must also belong to the operation that is still current.

08. A production failure in the first public release

The first Chrome Web Store release exposed another messaging issue.

After Visqora v0.4.0 was approved, I installed the published extension and opened the Side Panel.

The interface was completely blank.

The console reported an error equivalent to:

Cannot destructure property 'inspection'
as it is undefined.

Initially, this suggested a React initialization issue.

But the problem originated in communication with the background worker.

On startup, the Side Panel requested its initial state using GET_PANEL_STATE.

The published worker used an asynchronous chrome.runtime.onMessage listener that returned a Promise.

In the affected runtime, that approach didn't keep the response channel open as the implementation expected.

The Side Panel received undefined instead of the expected state, and the following React render crashed.

Correcting the runtime response contract

The corrected implementation uses Chrome's callback-based messaging contract.

For asynchronous work, the listener returns true synchronously and later responds through sendResponse.

Conceptually:

chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener(
  (message, sender, sendResponse) => {
    if (message.type !== 'GET_PANEL_STATE') {
      return false;
    }

    getPanelState()
      .then(sendResponse)
      .catch((error) => {
        sendResponse({
          error: String(error)
        });
      });

    return true;
  }
);

Illustrative code showing the asynchronous response-channel contract, not a direct extract from the repository.

The hotfix also strengthened response validation in the Side Panel.

Instead of assuming every message contains a valid state object, the interface now checks incoming responses and renders an explicit error when they are invalid.

Workspace restoration also handles empty, malformed, or unavailable session storage.

These improvements address the original failure while making unexpected communication problems easier to diagnose.

09. The real surprise: artifact drift

The investigation uncovered an additional problem.

The published v0.4.0 Side Panel bundle was byte-for-byte identical to the corresponding local bundle.

The background worker was not.

The callback-style response correction had already entered the repository after the Store artifact was created, inside an unrelated change.

As a result, the current local code behaved correctly while the published package still contained the faulty implementation.

The problem wasn't minification or an unexpected React production optimization.

We had been testing code that was different from the code users actually installed.

That changed the focus of the release process.

Instead of validating only the repository's current state, we needed to validate the exact production artifact being distributed.

10. Testing and releasing v0.4.1

The v0.4.1 hotfix concentrated on reliability.

We added regression coverage for:

  • Initial Side Panel rendering.
  • Missing and malformed worker responses.
  • Runtime response-channel behavior.
  • Empty and restored comparison workspaces.
  • Session-storage failures.
  • Asynchronous response success and failure.

The release passed 60 automated tests across eight files, along with linting, formatting, type checking, and production build verification.

We also tested the generated production extension in Chrome.

The final interactive checks were particularly important because headless testing couldn't fully reproduce every user permission interaction.

After testing, the corrected v0.4.1 package was submitted to the Chrome Web Store.

The published update was installed and verified successfully.

The lesson was broader than fixing a message listener.

The actual installation artifact is part of the software we need to test.

11. What I learned

A small browser extension can involve surprisingly rich architectural decisions.

Building Visqora reinforced several principles I value in frontend engineering.

Treat execution contexts as explicit boundaries

The React UI, service worker, and injected page code have different responsibilities and lifecycles.

Communication between them needs contracts, validation, and failure handling.

Keep a single owner for mutable state

Centralizing workspace mutations in the background worker simplifies consistency, even though it means state changes must cross a messaging boundary.

Separate live interactions from historical data

Inspection belongs to a specific document and session.

Captured snapshots can remain useful after that context disappears.

Keeping the two separate enables cross-page comparisons without pretending DOM elements live forever.

Design for privacy through data minimization

An inspector doesn't need to capture everything it can access.

Extracting a bounded set of properties reduces unnecessary data collection and clarifies the feature's purpose.

Test failures at integration boundaries

A successful unit test can't prove that Chrome messaging, extension permissions, and packaged assets behave correctly together.

The release artifact and the browser runtime must also be part of verification.

Keep product scope focused

Visqora isn't trying to replace DevTools, screenshot regression platforms, or design-system auditing tools.

It focuses on one problem: helping people inspect and compare implementation details efficiently.

12. What's next?

Visqora is still an early-stage tool.

For now, I'm focused on understanding how frontend developers, QA engineers, and designers use it in real workflows.

The extension is free and doesn't require an account.

Future improvements will depend on real feedback rather than adding features simply to expand the product.

Building Visqora has been a useful exercise in browser APIs, TypeScript contracts, state ownership, DOM inspection, asynchronous communication, and software distribution.

And if there's one lesson I'll carry into future releases, it's this:

The product is not the source code sitting in the repository. It's the software that users actually run.

Explore Visqora

Chrome Web Store: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/visqora/djjlhjglgjjaeafhekmejaeobfmhpngh

Product website: https://visqora.55onze.com

55onze: https://55onze.com

Gustavo A Roberto · Frontend Engineering, Architecture & Technical Leadership

articles.title: Which Session Is Waiting for Me? Claude Code Hooks on a Stream Deck
articles.description: I usually have several Claude Code sessions running side by side — a document here, a small fix...
articles.body_html:
I usually have several Claude Code sessions running side by side — a document here, a small fix there, some research. On a busy day, around five.

Delegating the work wasn't the problem. Noticing was:

  • A session asking "may I run this?" gets buried behind other windows.
  • A session finishes, and I don't notice for a while.
  • I keep switching windows just to check.

The AI wasn't the slow part. The time until I noticed was. The more sessions I ran, the worse it got.

The setup: three small pieces

I put the state of each session on a small button box on my desk (a Stream Deck Neo: 8 keys and a thin info bar).

  1. Claude Code hooks run a small script at fixed moments — a prompt is submitted, a tool is about to run, permission is requested, the turn stops.
  2. The script writes one tiny JSON file per session: which folder, which session, which state. No prompt text, no tool output.
  3. A Stream Deck plugin reads those files every second and colors the keys.

The hook side is mostly a mapping from hook events to four states:

// hook events -> key state
function stateFor(d) {
  switch (d.hook_event_name) {
    case "UserPromptSubmit":
    case "PostToolUse":
      return "running";                  // blue
    case "PreToolUse":                   // asking me a question also counts as waiting on me
      return ["AskUserQuestion", "ExitPlanMode"].includes(d.tool_name) ? "ask" : "running";
    case "PermissionRequest":
      return "ask";                      // red
    case "Notification":
      if (d.notification_type === "permission_prompt") return "ask";
      if (d.notification_type === "idle_prompt") return "waiting";
      return null;
    case "Stop":
      return "waiting";                  // orange: done, please look
    case "SessionStart":
      return "idle";                     // gray
    default:
      return null;
  }
}

The colors:

Color Meaning
Blue Working
Red Waiting for my permission
Orange Done — please look
Gray Idle

Pressing a key brings that session's window to the front. See red, press it, approve in that window. No more hunting.

Where it broke

The bug that took longest: a session finished, but its key stayed blue.

The hook writes to a temp file and renames it over the real one. The plugin reads that file every second. On Windows, if the rename lands at the exact moment the plugin is reading, the rename can fail with EPERM. My first version silently swallowed that error — so the "done" state was never written, and the key stayed blue. By the time I found it, 28 orphaned temp files had piled up.

The fix is boring: retry a few times with a short wait.

function replaceFile(tmp, file) {
  for (let i = 0; ; i++) {
    try { fs.renameSync(tmp, file); return; } catch (e) {
      if (i >= 9) { try { fs.unlinkSync(tmp); } catch {} throw e; }
      Atomics.wait(new Int32Array(new SharedArrayBuffer(4)), 0, 0, 30); // ~30 ms
    }
  }
}

Boring, but necessary. A status light you can't trust is just decoration.

Smaller one: after /clear, the session continues under a new ID, so I briefly had two keys with the same name. Now the hook removes the old record when a session starts from a clear, and keeps an old-ID → new-ID map for the plugin.

Then a character moved in

Colors alone felt a bit dry, so I drew a pixel-art chick into the keys. Her name is Aqui (from Aquila, the eagle constellation).

  • Working: juggling a ball
  • Waiting for permission: holding up a "?"
  • Done: a "!"
  • Idle: eyes closed, "z"

If the next key is also working, she passes the ball over. I wanted a box I like looking at, not just another notification.

That turned into a series of YouTube Shorts — over 20 episodes now. These days she rides around in a pixel-art WRX S4 through the seasons.

  • Shorts playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLOctjyutDnug
  • How it works (2:25, Japanese with visuals): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m7cUQ3Owqv0

If you only do one thing

Put "waiting for permission" somewhere you'll see it. It doesn't need a Stream Deck — a colored corner of the screen or a sound works. For me, the time a session spent waiting on me was the least visible and the most wasted.

I haven't measured how much time this saves, so I won't claim a number. What I can say is that I stopped hunting through windows.

Japanese version (note): https://note.com/modern_elk8749/n/n516084403556

A personal project by a Claude Code fan. Not affiliated with Anthropic or Elgato.
